fullText:
Kanishka Narayan to say Britain cannot rely entirely on tech companies amid rising global concern over AI dangers

Companies building the most advanced AI systems must increase safety efforts, the UK’s AI minister will say, as he announces a strengthening of Britain’s cyber defences.

Kanishka Narayan will call on companies developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. He will say Britain cannot rely entirely on technology companies to police their own models and will argue the UK needs to build more of its own AI infrastructure.

Narayan’s speech in west London will be the first since Andy Burnham made AI a cabinet-level brief. It comes as Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which tests the most powerful AI models, raised fears enemy states could steal unreleased cutting-edge models. Amid increasing global concern at dangers posed by AI, Irving told the Guardian: “The AI companies do not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models.”

He cited a recent incident at OpenAI where it was “hacked” by cybersecurity researchers, who said “the scope of what we could theoretically access was huge”. The attack was carried out under an OpenAI programme that rewarded ethical hackers testing its systems. OpenAI says it has multiple protections against theft of its models, including encryption and continuous monitoring.

Irving, a former employee at OpenAI and Google DeepMind who now runs an AI safety research body, has warned there is a “50% chance” of humanity being wiped out by superintelligent AIs and the only answer, for now, is to stop development of advanced systems as soon as possible. Irving is concerned by the rate of progress in alarming attributes shown by models, which could lead to them becoming highly advanced in traits such as concealing their actions and manipulating humans.

“It is possible we [will] get superintelligence in less than 12 months, on the current path,” he said.

Narayan’s speech will be watched closely for signs the UK may join a call for international governments to coordinate common safety standards for AIs, which has been signed by leaders of nations including Finland, France, Germany, Australia, Singapore, the UAE and Ireland, but not the UK and the US, where Donald Trump has said he wants the leading AI companies to “self-police”. The international alliance calling for strict rules comes after a wave of recent incidents with misaligned advanced AIs hacking into private and government systems.

In one of the latest cases, Anthropic on Friday revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model the AI contacted police claiming it could help solve a murder. It had landed on a page containing a police department tip form and a mention of an unsolved homicide. It wrote: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” Although Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, its instructions did not rule out form submissions.

Last week UK intelligence leaders from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ briefed the cabinet on AI’s threat to national security, according to the Sunday Times. The warning from the spy chiefs is being seen by some as encouragement for Burnham to grip the AI safety issue more firmly.

The prime minister told the UN last month that Britain would use its G20 presidency next year to champion agreement on AI safety with “a single set of global principles and standards”. But safety experts are calling for faster action to avert the most serious risks, which range from advanced AIs being used to mount a cyber-attack on essential infrastructure to the creation of novel bioweapons.

Meanwhile, Satya Nadella, the chair and chief executive of Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is an OpenAI shareholder, on Saturday called for AI models to be designed with an “emergency brake”. He said people needed to start from the principle of assuming advanced AI models posed an insider risk.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” he wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

title: Russian gymnasts still waiting for visas for world championships
description: Less than a week before the world gymnastics championships begin, Russia is still waiting for its visas needed to enter the Netherlands.
fullText:
Less than a week before the world gymnastics championships begin, Russia is still waiting for its visas needed to enter the Netherlands.

The Russians were supposed to leave for Rotterdam, the Netherlands, this weekend. But they pushed their departure back because they have not received visas from the Dutch government. The world championships begin Saturday, Oct. 17 with men's qualifying.

"The dates have shifted slightly," reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova said Saturday, Oct. 10, on her Telegram channel. "However, there is still plenty of time before the start, and we continue to train."

Russia faced a similar situation ahead of the European championships in Zagreb, Croatia in August. Nine members of the 65-person delegation, including Melnikova and fellow Tokyo Olympics gold medalist Viktoria Listunova, were initially denied visas. Most eventually received them, though Listunova did not.

The Russian women won the team title at Europeans with the men taking silver, and Melnikova and Anna Kalmykova went 1-2 in the all-around.

The uncertainty over Russia's visas shows how fraught the issue of its participation remains, more than four years after its athletes were largely banished from international sports in response to its unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. Though individual, neutral athletes have been allowed to compete since 2024, Russia could not send full teams to events until the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension in July.

The gymnastics world championships are the first major international event where the Russians have a full team. Russia sent full teams to the world championships for fencing, modern pentathlon and rhythmic gymnastics this summer, but none of those sports are as prominent as gymnastics.

Even if Russia makes it to Rotterdam, it will not be allowed to wear its flag or colors and will be called "WG2" in deference to the Dutch government, an ally of Ukraine.

These gymnastics world championships are the first opportunity countries have to qualify for LA28, with the top three getting spots at the Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. The Russian women are expected to be the biggest challenge to the U.S. women for the team title, with the Russian men also being a medal contender.

fullText:
BANGKOK, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Finance officials from around the world will gather in Bangkok this week under the shadow of a widening war in the Middle East, the biggest-ever energy supply shock and rising interest rates that together pose daunting risks to already-sluggish global economic growth.

The US-Israeli-led war with Iran, now in its eighth month, and its inflationary impact, will dominate the agenda and sideline conversations during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, being held ‌outside of Washington for the first time in three years.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told Reuters during a tour of the 300,000 square-meter Queen Sirikit National Convention Center on Sunday evening that 18,000 people were registered to attend the meetings, 4,000 more than the ‌last off-site meetings held in Morocco in October 2023.

SEVERAL FINANCE MINISTERS STAYING AWAY

Notably absent will be US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who dispatched two senior officials in his stead while he handles some "domestic engagements," a US official said. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh will attend and is slated to participate in a public event with Georgieva on October 16.

Several other ​finance ministers were also staying home due to domestic budget and election duties, but most central bankers would attend, Georgieva said.

Bessent's decision to skip the high-profile gathering and a meeting of the Group of 20 major economies, which the U.S. leads this year, may frustrate counterparts amid rising tensions over the Iran war, Ukraine's battle against Russia's invasion and the U.S. move to impose sanctions on the International Criminal Court.

World Bank President Ajay Banga told Reuters that while global growth had held up better than feared when Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, shutting off some 20% of the world's oil, pressures were building again. Soaring prices for diesel, rising fertilizer prices and a looming "super" El Niño weather effect that experts say could lead to 450,000 heat-related deaths are all hitting at once.

Group of Seven countries have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, ‌who is keen to see lower gasoline prices before November elections that could see his Republican Party ⁠lose control of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced a deal with Russia that would provide even more diesel to global markets and a temporary waiver of U.S. sanctions designed to deprive Moscow of revenues for its war on Ukraine. The move drew swift criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy.

More than 1 billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of the war on February 28, but industry executives say the amount of ⁠oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, making the market more fragile and fueling pressure on prices.

Banga said the Bank was not revising down its global forecasts at the moment, but was keeping a close eye on developments. "The real thing is not just El Niño by itself; it's the combination ... What's happening to fertilizer prices? What's happening to energy costs? What's happening to debt? It's that put together that creates its own challenges," he said. "And I think that will call upon all of us to be far more careful on what we prepare for in the coming months."

IMF chief Georgieva issued a similar warning in ​her ​traditional curtain-raiser speech previewing the meetings last week, telling the audience: "Winter is coming."

The IMF has signaled little change in its forecast for 3% global growth in 2026 and ​may edge its forecast for next year slightly higher. But some countries will see downgrades, including Ukraine, now in ‌its fifth year of war against Russia's invasion, and Gulf countries hit by Iranian strikes and sharply reduced energy exports.

IMF research released on Tuesday showed that sharp spikes in food and energy prices are an increasingly common source of crises that drive inflation expectations higher for longer, worsen poverty and threaten economic stability.

One huge headache for policymakers is the growing public debt burden that is sapping growth and adding inflationary pressures. The IMF says public debt is at the highest level since World War Two and will exceed 100% of GDP before 2030.

Advanced economies, led by the United States, have the highest debt-to-GDP ratios, but emerging markets and low-income countries are particularly vulnerable, given a perfect storm of challenges: capital outflows in search of higher US rates, El Niño, and lack of investment in AI, which has mitigated negative supply shocks in the US and other rich countries.

Developing countries are particularly vulnerable given high public debt levels that will have to be renegotiated at higher interest rates. Together, they face $400 billion in debt payments to external creditors in 2026, and interest payments already exceed 10% of revenue on average.

Early in the COVID crisis, G20 leaders announced a suspension of debt ‌service payments for the poorest countries, but there is little appetite for such action now, according to diplomats from G20 countries, who said high debt levels and political ​pressures posed bigger hurdles this time.

Many lower-income countries are worried about new IMF recommendations for loan programs that call for fewer, but deeper reforms as a condition for approving ​lending, a change that many fear will lead to painful austerity measures.

"Countries are already cutting their expenditures because their debt payments are going ​high and because of the IMF conditionality," said Iolanda Fresnillo, who works on debt justice for Eurodad. "We fear that this review of conditionality policy is just going to make things worse."

Kenya, she said, had avoided a debt restructuring by cutting ‌public expenditures and trying to raise taxes, but the changes sparked significant protests, especially by the young.

The IMF ​risked losing credibility unless it acknowledged the severity of the crisis facing many ​developing countries.

"As long as they continue with the governance structure that they have, they are becoming less and less relevant," she said.

Flight routes to Bangkok often route through the Middle East, posing immediate security challenges to global travelers descending on Thailand's bustling capital city of 9 million residents following recent attacks on Saudi airports.

The last off-site annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank took place in Morocco just days after militants led by Hamas killed 1,200 people in Israel, followed by Israel's bombardment of Gaza that killed more than ​74,000 people and devastated cities throughout the Palestinian area.

Three years later, the linkage between national security and international finance ‌is clear, although finance officials at the time had dismissed the Hamas attack as not being an economic issue, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council.

"Obviously there have been massive global ramifications," he said. "What we're currently experiencing ​with Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has a direct connection with what happened three years ago."

Policymakers needed to become more agile in responding to geopolitical crises in an increasingly interconnected world, Lipsky said. "They have to be proactive ​and they have to recognize that they don't live in the world they used to."

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to "immediately reverse course" on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices.

Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," they wrote.

The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.

Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press," said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan.

"We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied," Tillis said.

Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine.

The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war.

"Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. "President Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law."

Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law.

"The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions," Barrasso said on CBS's "Face the Nation."

He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month.

"This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world," Barrasso said.

Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has elevated world energy prices.

title: Puerto Rican boxing legend Gomez dies aged 69
description: Three-weight world champion Wilfredo 'Bazooka' Gomez dies aged 69.
fullText:
Three-weight world champion Wilfredo 'Bazooka' Gomez has died aged 69.

The Puerto Rican won the WBC super-bantamweight title, WBC featherweight belt and WBA super-featherweight crown during a career in which he was renowned as a heavy puncher.

Gomez fought in 48 fights and won 44, with 42 by virtue of knockout, and was inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame, external in 1995.

Former president of the sanctioning body the WBO Paco Valcarcel confirmed the passing of his compatriot.

"He passed away a few hours ago, the one to whom I owe having entered the great family of international boxing," wrote Valcacel on social media on Saturday.

"Rest in peace, my eternal champion Wilfredo 'Bazooka' Gomez."

Gomez's best wins came against fellow greats Mexico's Carlos Zarate, two-weight champion Lupe Pintor, domestic rival Juan Laporte and American Rocky Lockridge.

Zarate was his finest win, stopping the then 52-0 knockout specialist in five rounds in front of his home fans in San Juan to retain his WBC super-bantamweight title.

Competing during a stacked era of talent at his weights, Gomez suffered heartbreak in two of his biggest fights when he was knocked out by Salvador Sanchez in 1981 and Azumah Nelson in 1984 - both at featherweight for the WBC world title.

The WBC and its president Mauricio Sulaiman called Gomez "one of the greatest icons in the history of the sport" and that he had passed away "after being hospitalised for the past two weeks due to respiratory complications".

"Universally recognized as one of the greatest ring legends of all time and a ruthless brawler who holds the historic record of 17 consecutive super bantamweight title defenses - all won by knockout - Wilfredo Gomez leaves behind an indelible legacy both inside and outside the ring," a statement said., external

As an amateur, Gomez competed at the 1972 Olympics aged just 15 and at 17 would win gold at the inaugural World Amateur Championships in Cuba.

title: Hamilton apologises to Ferrari as Antonelli moves to brink of title
description: Lewis Hamilton's incorrect strategy call during the Singapore Grand Prix means Kimi Antonelli can win the world title at the next race in Austin.
fullText:
Lewis Hamilton apologised to his Ferrari team after overriding the pit wall and choosing his own strategy during the Singapore Grand Prix.

Ferrari were on course to finish second and third with Charles Leclerc and Hamilton, but instead the seven-time champion fell back to sixth in the closing laps as he fought a losing battle to hold off three cars while on fading tyres.

Hamilton apologised to the team over the radio on the slowing-down lap after the race, saying: "Sorry, boys. I let you down today with that strategy. My call, and I lost us valuable points. I'll try and make up for it in the next one."

Team principal Frederic Vasseur said: "Clearly we asked them to pit. Charles pitted. Lewis didn't want to pit because he... I don't know why. And then he realised it was the wrong call. It's why he apologised to the team.

"Now it's not a drama for me that he made the wrong call. I'm making mistakes, he's making mistakes, we're all making mistakes sometimes. Now we have to look ahead and make mistakes positively."

Verstappen dominates for first Singapore Grand Prix win

Verstappen perfect and Antonelli hugely mature - driver ratings

Hamilton did not speak to the media after the race after saying he felt unwell and being given permission to miss the interview zone, known as the media pen.

In a statement released by Ferrari, he said: "Under the virtual safety car, the team called me in but I missed the entry. After that, I decided to stay out and try to hold track position to the end but in the closing laps, I was struggling massively with tyre degradation and lost three places, finishing P6, which doesn't reflect the pace we had in the car.

"A painful lesson, but I take full responsibility for the decisions I made. Not every call will work out, and I can accept getting it wrong but I'm sorry for the team for the points we lost today. They put so much into every weekend, and I wanted to deliver more for them. I'll continue to put the work in and come back fighting at the next race."

Ferrari called both cars in to the pits during a virtual safety car that was called mid-race. Stopping under the VSC saves about 10 seconds versus stopping under racing conditions.

Hamilton said in the statement that his decision was based on his improved pace on the soft-compound tyre after he had been forced to make an earlier pit stop than planned because the medium tyre on which he started the race was not performing.

"At a track (where it's) difficult to overtake, you need to try something different and I chose to start on a new medium tyre, to go long and try to make a one-stop work," he said.

"Unfortunately the medium didn't perform as well as the soft. I had a good second stint and the pace was back, but I couldn't make the progress I needed."

His first stop was six laps before Leclerc's and when the Monegasque emerged back on to the track, Hamilton was right behind him and was initially faster.

At one stage, he pointed out to the team that he had "lost two seconds on that lap", but the team decided not to invert the cars. Hamilton followed Leclerc within two seconds for a further 10 laps before slowly starting to lose ground a couple of laps before the VSC.

Vasseur said the team decided to leave Leclerc in front because he had pitted later than Hamilton.

"The tyre advantage was for Charles, that he pitted six laps later," Vasseur said. "I think it was the right call."

However, that argument appears to be somewhat undermined by the fact that the medium tyre emerged as the worst option for the race - as Hamilton had found out in the first stint and other drivers found later on.

Leclerc was put back on the soft when he stopped under the VSC.

Hamilton's error means Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli is in a position to clinch his first world title at the next race, the US Grand Prix in Austin, after finishing third behind race winner Max Verstappen and Leclerc.

Antonelli's lead over team-mate George Russell, who finished ninth after starting from the back of the grid, has extended to 102 points and 111 over Hamilton.

The Italian needs to leave Austin with an advantage of at least 125 points to clinch the title, with five races at most remaining after that.

He will do so if he wins the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower at the Circuit of the Americas on 25 October.

If he becomes champion this year, the 20-year-old will be the youngest in Formula 1 history.

Asked if he would be daring to dream about the title on the flight home, he said: "For sure, but at the same time, I know it's very close, I know it's there, but I just need to make sure that I keep doing the best I can.

"The mindset is always the same, to go out there and win and perform the best way I can.

"This weekend I haven't particularly driven that well. I felt like I could have done a better job, but I feel confident that a week to reset and I'm really looking forward to being back in Austin.

"But at the end of the day, if I don't do my job well, then the result won't come. So in order to achieve what I want, I need to perform, as simple as that."

There is some doubt about the mathematics of the championship because it is not completely clear how many races are remaining.

F1 is pushing ahead with the original schedule, which ends with two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, despite the war in the Middle East, having been reassured the countries are safe.

But if the war intensifies before mid-November, those races will have to be cancelled. In that event, the season would end at Imola in Italy, on the same 6 December date as Abu Dhabi, after a two-week break following the Las Vegas race on 22 November.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "I haven't looked at it from that perspective, because the moment I have the thought of 'how many points is it actually, and when could he win it,' I remind myself that this is motor racing and crazy things have happened.

"The aim must be to score points, not to lose too many on the others, like today, gaining on Lewis, which was unexpected, and then it's going to come towards him, whether that's in Mexico or Brazil (the races immediately after Austin) or further down the line."

Mercedes split their cars between two different specifications in Singapore in an attempt to understand why a major upgrade introduced at the previous race in Malaysia did not work.

Antonelli drove the new spec and Russell the old, and by the end of the weekend the team said they had made some progress in understanding the new aerodynamic package.

Antonelli said: "We're just trying to understand how to extract more potential out of it because we do see the gains, we do see what it could bring.

"It's just that the window is very small at the moment where the car operates and is very sensitive to the way you drive it, the way you take a corner, the way you brake. So it reacts very differently.

"So hopefully now in Austin, we have three free practices, so we can be very open-minded with set-up and hopefully we can find a way and we can use the full potential of the package and finally see the gains."

Russell was asked how he viewed the rest of the season now the championship was almost over. He replied: "The goal is to improve the car. We were dominant for so long and since the break we have seen Red Bull be exceptionally fast on many different types of circuits and we need to go back to winning ways."

Verstappen's victory was his first grand prix win in Singapore. It was also his second in succession, emphasising Red Bull's return to the front after a difficult start to the season.

Verstappen said: "Very different tracks that we have gone well at now. That's of course always nice to see.

"Our car has taken a really nice step forward. It's just been more driveable and more predictable. That's what I wanted and needed from the car to find that last step to fight up front. And I hope that we can carry that momentum forward.

"We don't really have anything to win in the championship, right? Kimi is miles ahead. I don't care if I'm second, third or fourth. It doesn't do anything. But I just want to have fun until the end, you know, try to go for a day's success."

But the four-time champion was cautious about the prospect of being competitive at every race before the end of the season.

"It's very difficult to say and I don't want to say now that I will be in the fight in Austin," he said.

"Yeah, the last few weekends have been great. But I just take it race by race and once we are in Austin, then we'll see how it will go there. But it's again a very different track.

"From what I saw in WEC (the World Endurance Championship), the track is incredibly bumpy. Oh my God, yeah, I'll probably need to order a new spine, I think, after the weekend. Yeah, I'll become like Robocop. Yeah, crazy. That's again a new challenge for everyone, to deal with those bumps.

"And then we just go from there. We have to go to Mexico, high altitude, everything will run super hot, and we need to see how the engine is going to perform in that altitude, how the car is behaving, because it's very different.

"So there are so many different things that you can get right or wrong in those races."

Hughes focused on Albania before World Cup dream
description: Wales forward Elise Hughes admits reaching the World Cup would fulfil a lifelong ambition.
fullText:
Wales forward Elise Hughes says the prospect of reaching the World Cup would fulfil a lifelong ambition but insists the focus remains on Tuesday's play-off second leg against Albania.

Rhian Wilkinson's side take a slender 1-0 advantage into the return fixture in Llanelli after edging the first leg of their play-off semi-final.

A draw would be enough to send Wales through to the next stage of qualifying for next summer's tournament in Brazil.

"When you're a kid, it doesn't get bigger than that," Hughes said of playing at a World Cup.

"You dream and you're in the garden thinking of the World Cup and you're at your grassroots team thinking of the World Cup.

"Now this group has a chance to do it and that is the most important thing for the group here and now.

"But to do that, we've got to win the game on Tuesday. This is the most important game to date because it's next."

Should Wales overcome Albania, they will face either Norway or Romania in a two-legged play-off final in December.

Even if Wales win that play-off final they could face a potential inter-confederation play-off in February.

Head coach Wilkinson acknowledged her side will need to improve in Llanelli after an unconvincing 1-0 first-leg victory in Shkoder.

"There's always room for improvement," Sunderland's Hughes told BBC Sport Wales.

"We've won games by many more goals and always had room for improvement.

"We knew they're a good side and what they're going to bring [but] we let them into the game. It's all about focus and getting the result."

title: Trump weighs joining Saudi strikes as Riyadh airport is hit for a second straight day
description:
— A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.
Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday’s missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday.
fullText:
CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others.

Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights. Saturday's missile attack was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began, with another 300 people wounded, some critically. The airport was still closed Sunday.

The sharp escalation in the new front in the war threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement, as President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no immediate White House comment Sunday.

The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis.

At stake, again, in this escalation are global supplies and prices of oil as well as commercial shipping through a crucial alternative waterway to the Iran-threatened Strait of Hormuz — along with civilians and aviation throughout the region.

Trump on Saturday also said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who has been seeking assistance.

A U.S. intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen and further restrict the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month and the Saudi-led coalition has been trying to seize them back.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told The Associated Press last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Sunday's attack occurred as the Saudis hosted a major international energy conference in Riyadh, with other high-profile events including an investment gathering on the horizon. Saudi Arabia under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has sought to open more to the world as a business and tourism destination, but the Houthi attacks threaten those efforts.

"There is no way that somebody will break our back. We are like a phoenix, we come out of the ashes all the time," the Saudi energy minister, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud, told the conference.

He added that the kingdom is also working on pipelines in addition to the East-West one that was attacked and closed for days last month, with no details.

Earlier Sunday, the Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa. The ministry also said 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in five weeks, 60% of them women and children.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

On Sunday, the Houthis also claimed attacks on King Fahd Airport in the city of Damma, as well as oil and gas facilities in the kingdom's east. They have targeted the Riyadh airport, which has no military facilities, every day since Wednesday.

The rebels again warned "all airlines, experts, employees, workers and ​travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our ​forces." Several international airlines have suspended flights for varying periods.

Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the group's military spokesperson, wrote on X that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, however, were exempt. The kingdom earlier called Mecca a "red line."

A Saudi statement said the dead in Saturday's attack included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.

The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, who worked for Saudi airline Flynas, according to Egyptian state-run TV.

The Syrian woman was a widowed mother of four who had been living in Saudi Arabia for five years, relative Nisreen Oweida told The Associated Press. The Syrian Embassy identified her as Buthaina Ahmad Oweida.

Until recently, the Houthis had been largely on the sidelines of the Iran war, but they have developed their military capabilities in recent years to become one of Tehran's most powerful allies. Now, the rebels are helping Iran to pressure a key U.S. ally.

The Saudis and the Houthis began fighting in 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war on behalf of the internationally recognized government. Relative calm after a 2022 ceasefire ended in July when the Houthis resumed attacks, saying the Saudis fired on the Sanaa airport as a plane from Iran was trying to land.

That revived anger over the Saudi-led blockade that has largely isolated Houthi-run areas. The Houthis say they have now imposed a blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Fighting has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains near the Bab el-Mandeb, a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

But Ahmed Nagi, the International Crisis Group's senior analyst for Yemen, said the Houthi pressure tactics could backfire. "Rather than pushing Riyadh to step back, attacks on critical Saudi infrastructure could make the Saudis more determined to continue the campaign," he said.

A previous version of this report has been corrected to show that the Egyptian killed in the strike was a woman, not a man.

Frankel and Anna reported from Jerusalem. Associated Press writers Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Collin Binkley in Washington, Sally Abou AlJoud in Beirut and Omar Albam in Maarat al-Numan, Syria, contributed to this report.

title: ‘Humiliation ritual’ – WWE fans aren’t buying Triple H’s LA Knight comments after Roman Reigns loss

fullText:
LA Knight came up short yet again in his quest to win a world championship, losing to Roman Reigns in the opening match of Money in the Bank.

Despite being a crowd favourite and one of the biggest, most organically grown stars in recent memory, the WWE have done little to reward LA Knight for his hard work.

Outside of a run with the United States championship in 2024, Knight has found himself in a perennial bridesmaid role with the company, constantly failing to win the world title.

In the Money in the Bank post-show, WWE Chief Content Officer Paul 'Triple H' Levesque praised LA Knight for his performances against Roman Reigns.

Despite him not winning the World Heavyweight Championship, Triple H claimed Knight showed that he proved he is a main-event player.

Triple H said: "LA Knight, to me, left this match greater than he went in. LA Knight proved that he is a megastar.

"LA Knight proved that he belongs in that title scene. LA Knight proved that he is a top attraction in this business."

While these are positive comments from the head booker of the company, fans were understandably frustrated that this outward praise from Levesque rarely translated to the on-screen product.

One fan wrote: "What he is saying is a complete lie compared to how he booked Knight in the match."

Another fan added, "He has said this before, and LA Knight ended up in the lower midcard."

A third fan made a scathing comment about Levesque's booking of LA Knight: "It's just a humiliation ritual at this point. He's doing it to troll all of his fans. That's the only reason why he made this match – for his yearly Money in the Bank humiliation ritual. It's embarrassing to watch."

Amid frustration and concern about Knight's future, a fourth fan wrote: "LA Knight is soon to be 44 and looks no more likely to win a world title in WWE than he did yesterday. Should've been strapped up years ago, but they still refuse to do it."

A fifth fan pointed to a historic pattern within the company: "The thing with WWE is they hate it when you make yourself a star, especially when they didn't plan it. Unfortunately for LA Knight, they still don't plan on it."

And lastly, one final fan hoped for a more optimistic result for Knight in the future: "LA Knight better be getting a WrestleMania coronation when he wins the World Title at this stage."

Knight has been one of the WWE's most popular stars since he caught fire in 2023. While he has yet to win a world title, he has proved himself to be quite valuable for the company as one of their most reliable babyfaces.

There is some truth to the idea that the WWE brain trust doesn't reward wrestlers for organically getting over, with Zack Ryder (Matt Cardona) and Daniel Bryan (Bryan Danielson) being prime examples.

And while this isn't the same regime that tried to squash the previous two examples, a lot of their habits are very similar to the way Vince McMahon would react in those situations.

title: Bryson DeChambeau Weighs Options Beyond LIV Golf
description: Bryson DeChambeau explores career paths outside LIV Golf, including the DP World Tour and YouTube, as the league faces restructuring uncertainty.
fullText:
Bryson DeChambeau is looking beyond the current LIV Golf structure as the league faces a major business overhaul. The two-time major champion has been linked to more starts on the DP World Tour, signaling a potential shift in his competitive schedule.

While he remains under contract, the uncertainty surrounding the league's future has opened the door for other options. This includes a confirmed appearance in South Africa later this year and a serious push to grow his digital media presence if the tour model changes.

The situation is fluid, with several high-profile players making moves to secure their futures. Jon Rahm has already stated he will not participate in the proposed LIV 2.0 plan, and Sergio Garcia was granted a release from his contract earlier this week.

Golf Channel reported that John Beck, representing Rahm, stated at a bankruptcy hearing that Rahm had "independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0" and deemed them "unacceptable to him." This leaves DeChambeau as a key figure whose decision could define the new league.

Reports from The Telegraph indicate that DeChambeau's team has contacted DP World Tour officials to discuss potential tournament appearances in 2027. Late last month, golf insider Alan Shipnuck noted that DeChambeau continued to consider his options.

Unlike Patrick Reed, who joined the European tour when he departed LIV at the start of 2026, this American is not seeking full membership on that circuit. Instead, he appears to be looking for specific starts rather than a full roster commitment.

DeChambeau has also been vocal about his business ventures. Stating in May 2026 to Golf Channel that he aimed to triple his YouTube audience should LIV Golf fail to continue. At the time, his channel had approximately 2.69 million subscribers.

He mentioned plans to expand videos into additional languages to reach a global audience. An interview from 2025 disclosed his investment of over $1 million in his YouTube operation, demonstrating a serious commitment to this alternative revenue stream.

The most concrete step away from the current LIV model is his scheduled participation in the Nedbank Golf Challenge. The DP World Tour confirmed DeChambeau's entry in August. From December 3 to 6, 2026, he will compete at the Gary Player Country Club in Sun City, South Africa. This event provides a guaranteed competitive platform outside the LIV circuit before the end of the 2026 season. It serves as a clear indicator that he is keeping his options open while the league's future remains unclear.

The landscape for elite golfers is shifting rapidly as players evaluate their long-term careers. DeChambeau's hesitation to commit to LIV 2.0 mirrors the sentiment of other top players who are wary of the league's restructuring. The DP World Tour is increasingly positioning itself as a lifeline for those seeking an exit. While DeChambeau has not announced a permanent departure, his actions speak to a desire for flexibility.

His strategy seems to focus on maintaining high-level competition through select events while building a media empire that does not rely on a single tour. This dual approach allows him to stay relevant in the sport regardless of how the business side resolves.

The investment in YouTube suggests he is preparing for a future where his audience might be more valuable than his tournament purse. If LIV 2.0 fails to secure enough players with outstanding financial claims, the pressure on DeChambeau to make a final choice will only increase.

For now, the focus remains on the upcoming tournament in South Africa. The Nedbank Golf Challenge runs from December 3 to 6, 2026, offering a clear date for fans to watch DeChambeau in action outside the LIV framework.

This appearance was confirmed by the DP World Tour in August and stands as the only fixed competitive commitment outside the league at this moment. Any further moves will likely depend on how the bankruptcy proceedings and the LIV 2.0 deadline unfold.

title: 5 Explosive Reasons To Watch ONE SAMURAI 4 On October 17
description: Fans inside Ariake Arena and those around the world are in for an electric night of martial arts action in Tokyo.
fullText:
ONE Championship brings one of its biggest shows of the year back to Tokyo, and the card has the absolute star power to match the special occasion.

ONE SAMURAI 4 lands at the iconic Ariake Arena on Saturday, October 17, with explosive bouts across Muay Thai, kickboxing, submission grappling, and MMA.

The lineup features the best of Japan, from established warriors to hungry up-and-comers, alongside a world-class international contingent eager to crash the party on Japanese soil.

From the first bell to the last, here are five electrifying reasons to circle the date as the world's largest martial arts organization returns to "The Land of the Rising Sun" this week.

Jonathan "The General" Haggerty arrives in Tokyo for the third defense of his ONE Bantamweight Kickboxing World Title, and the Englishman carries himself like a man who has yet to meet his match in the sport.

The 29-year-old is widely regarded as one of the best pound-for-pound strikers on the planet. A former ONE Flyweight and Bantamweight Muay Thai World Champion, he added a third belt to his collection by flattening Fabricio "Wonder Boy" Andrade in the second round at ONE Fight Night 16 in November 2023.

Since then, he has remained unbeaten in kickboxing inside ONE, with defenses against Wei Rui and, most recently, Yuki Yoza in a five-round war at ONE SAMURAI 1.

Standing in his way is a man who knows exactly what it feels like to sit on that throne. Hiroki Akimoto captured the crown with a solid five-round display back at ONE X in March 2022 before enduring a difficult stretch after losing it.

2025 brought the turnaround, though, with wins over former ONE Bantamweight MMA World Champion John "Hands of Stone" Lineker and Wei, followed by a split decision over fellow Japanese dynamo Taimu Hisai earlier this year that confirmed him as the rightful challenger.

A perfect kickboxing run on one side, a former king chasing his old throne on the other, and a home crowd behind the challenger: these are the ingredients of a World Title fight fans will be talking about for years.

Reigning ONE Atomweight Muay Thai World Champion Nadaka Yoshinari steps in for his second assignment as the divisional king with a 42-fight winning streak and more than seven years without a loss.

The 25-year-old claimed the inaugural belt against Thai standout Numsurin Chor Ketwina at ONE 173 in November last year, then outpointed longtime rival Songchainoi "Mini-Hulk" Kiatsongrit across five fast-paced rounds at ONE SAMURAI 1.

Blinding speed, southpaw precision, and defensive mastery have made him one of the most technically gifted fighters of the modern era, but he could be forced to work extra hard as he chases a 43rd consecutive win against the dangerous Rifdean "Magic Boy" Masdor.

The 23-year-old knockout artist has been nearly flawless under the ONE banner. The Malaysian striker carries a 7-1 record, five straight wins, a 71 percent finish rate, and an average fight time of just four and a half minutes. His latest outing, a first-round finish of Javad Mozafari, earned him a life-changing US$100,000 main roster contract.

For Nadaka, the stakes are historic. Another successful defense would further cement his place among the greatest Muay Thai athletes Japan has ever produced.

The stakes are far bigger in the opposite corner: handing the Eiwa Sports Gym product his first defeat in years would make Rifdean only the second ONE World Champion from Malaysia, following in the footsteps of recently crowned interim strawweight Muay Thai king Aliff Sor Dechapan.

Pair a dominant streak that long with a fighter built to finish, and fireworks are inevitable.

Between the two marquee World Title fights, ONE SAMURAI 4 hosts four of the most dangerous kickboxers in the world — all thirsting for glory in the semifinals of the prestigious ONE SAMURAI Featherweight Kickboxing Tournament.

Three-time Glory Kickboxing World Champion Marat Grigorian meets "The Handsome White Dragon" Luo Chao in the first of the two highly anticipated matchups. The 35-year-old Armenian powerhouse arrives with 71 career wins built on his hallmark pressure, heavy hands, and an intimidating aura.

He booked his spot in the final four with a crushing unanimous decision over Mamuka Usubyan at The Inner Circle 25. Luo, meanwhile, showed his resolve at ONE SAMURAI 2 just a day later, surviving a tough middle stretch against Kosuke "Unstoppable Phoenix" Takagi before breaking through with a late barrage to take the decision.

The other side of the bracket brings its own brand of chaos as former ONE Interim Featherweight Kickboxing World Champion Masaaki Noiri locks horns against Iranian bruiser Mohammad Siasarani.

Noiri stormed through his quarterfinal with a first-round knockout of "Spirit Dragon" Liu Mengyang, avenging an earlier loss and taking home a US$100,000 bonus. The 24-year-old Siasarani, on the other hand, delivered a highlight-reel moment of his own with a stunning head kick finish of Kaito in his 10th promotional triumph.

A spot in the final is on the line, and the tournament winner will earn the prestigious silver belt and a guaranteed shot at reigning ONE Featherweight Kickboxing World Champion Superbon.

Whichever way the bracket shakes out, fans are guaranteed non-stop entertainment here.

Tokyo could hand out more than wins on this card, because the next challengers for 26 pounds of gold may be decided right here across two high-stakes kickboxing battles.

Yuki Yoza meets Nabil Anane in a bantamweight showdown with heavy World Title implications. The former K-1 Champion, who capped a 3-0 run in ONE with a dominant win over "The Kicking Machine" Superlek, came up short against Haggerty at ONE SAMURAI 1 but bounced back with an impressive unanimous decision over Ben "The Problem" Woolliss this past July.

Anane, the former ONE Bantamweight Muay Thai World Champion, brings his towering 6-foot-4 stature and versatile striking to a matchup that pits Yoza's precision and calf kicks against reach. A win would put either man in the conversation for the divisional gold.

In lightweight kickboxing action, Rukiya "Demolition Man" Anpo returns for his sophomore ONE outing after falling short against Grigorian in his debut at ONE 173 inside the same venue. The former K-1 Champion has the hands and the power to make a statement, and he is eager to show he belongs on this stage as he moves up to lightweight.

Standing in his way is Bulgarian tank Bogdan Shumarov, who has looked nothing short of entertaining throughout his tenure on the global stage. The hard-hitting striker has wrapped all his promotional victories in highlight-reel fashion, so don't be surprised if another follows suit.

Waiting at the top is two-sport ONE Lightweight World Champion Regian "The Immortal" Eersel, and whoever wins will make a strong case for the next chance at his gold.

Different divisions, same prize: a seat at the table when the next World Title fights are made.

Few names carry more weight in Japanese combat sports than Takeru "Natural Born Krusher" Segawa, and ONE SAMURAI 4 gives him the send-off he deserves.

The three-division K-1 Champion retired with a 46-5 record after stopping Rodtang "The Iron Man" Jitmuangnon in the fifth round to win the ONE Interim Flyweight Kickboxing World Championship at ONE SAMURAI 1. He will be inducted into the ONE Hall of Fame and receive a 10-gong salute.

He is the fourth name to receive the honor, following fellow ex-ONE World Champions Demetrious "Mighty Mouse" Johnson, Bibiano "The Flash" Fernandes, and "The Burmese Python" Aung La N Sang.

While "Natural Born Krusher" takes his place in history, the rest of Japan's best will be competing with something to prove. Itsuki "Android 18" Hirata is looking to make a statement when she runs it back with Malaysian rival Jihin "Shadow Cat" Radzuan in atomweight MMA action.

K-1 Champion Shintaro Matsukura, meanwhile, opens his promotional account in a lightweight kickboxing bout against former ONE Lightweight Muay Thai World Title challenger Sinsamut "Aquaman" Klinmee.

In addition to that, a quartet of all-Japanese matchups should get the night off to a flyer. Shozo "Great Teacher" Isojima takes on Kota Abe in lightweight MMA, Toki Tamaru faces Shoma Okumura in strawweight kickboxing, Yu Takeuchi and Ryoto Nishiyama duke it out in flyweight MMA, while Yoshinari Fukushima meets Masaki Takeura in lightweight submission grappling.

title: Bezzecchi wins as Martin retakes championship lead
description: Marco Bezzecchi triumphs at the Indonesian Grand Prix, while Jorge Martin finishes third to retake the lead from Marc Marquez in the MotoGP world championship.
fullText:
Marco Bezzecchi triumphed at the Indonesian Grand Prix, while Jorge Martin finished third to retake the lead from Marc Marquez in the MotoGP world championship.

Italian Bezzecchi made his move on pole-sitter Raul Fernandez with nine laps to go at a sweltering Mandalika International Circuit.

Fernandez finished second ahead of compatriot Martin, with the Spanish duo locking out the podium for Italian manufacturer Aprilia.

Ducati's reigning seven-time world champion Marquez finished sixth, losing the championship lead he had taken for the first time this season by winning Saturday's sprint race.

Fernandez and Bezzecchi had clashed and crashed out in that race, with the Spaniard needing to brake with his middle finger for the whole of Sunday's race after fracturing his index finger.

Starting at the front of the grid, the pair negotiated the first turn and then surged away from the chasing pack.

Having initially looked comfortable, Fernandez began to fade and Bezzecchi seized an opportunity on lap 19 before putting distance on his rival.

The result for 2024 world champion Martin moves him up to 355 points at the top of the championship standings, with Marquez second on 353 and Bezzecchi third with 309.

There are five grands prix remaining in the 2026 season, with the Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island the next meeting in the calendar in a fortnight's time.

fullText:
At least 12 people were killed and hundreds wounded when Yemen’s Houthi militants struck Riyadh’s international airport with a missile on Saturday, in Saudi Arabia’s deadliest attack in more than a decade.

It was the third missile strike this week on the King Khalid International Airport, which has been closed until at least late Sunday, leading to the cancellation of more than 600 flights.

The missile struck a terminal building, killing four Saudis, two Bangladeshis, an American, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian, a Palestinian, and a Sudanese, the kingdom’s civil aviation body said Sunday, adding that 309 people were wounded.

Following the attack, US President Donald Trump said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis in Yemen, having previously resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention.

One traveler told Reuters news agency they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed.

Another recalled hearing an explosion before seeing several people lying wounded on the ground.

An eyewitness video released by Reuters showed large boards and debris strewn across the terminal floor, with people moving through a dust-filled hall.

King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia’s second-busiest, serves the capital, Riyadh, a city of about eight million people.

Nasr al-Din Amer, a senior Houthi official, appeared to acknowledge responsibility, writing on X: “We shut down Riyadh international airport.”

The US, UK, Spain and Canada are among countries warning their citizens against using the airport.

Saturday’s incident has exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom’s defense capabilities as it wages an air campaign in support of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, which is fighting the Houthis on the ground.

With Iranian assistance, the Houthis have built up a large arsenal of missiles, including ballistic weapons, as well as a range of drones.

A Houthi military statement Sunday reiterated a warning to all airlines and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, “as they are vulnerable to targeting… with the exception of Mecca and Medina airports.”

“Saudi Arabia will bear responsibility for any failed attempts to intercept” missiles, the Houthi statement said, and it would continue responding to “blockades with blockades, and escalation with escalation.”

The group has also warned airliners against using Saudi airspace.

Trump said Saturday he plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman following the attack.

“They’re able to defend. The Saudis are good fighters. But I think the attack was a terrible thing,” Trump said when asked whether Saudi Arabia could defend itself against the Houthis.

Asked outside the White House whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis, a militia aligned with US foe Iran, Trump told reporters: “We may. We’re going to look at it.”

“We just found out about the recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”

Last month, Trump rejected two appeals from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for US strikes against the Houthis, CNN reported at the time.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a US citizen was among those killed and condemned the attacks as showing “a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life,” in a post on X.

Wounded people, including some in critical condition, were rushed to hospitals Saturday by ambulance and helicopter, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Two previous attacks at the airport this week killed four people and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane.

UN Special Envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg called the attacks “a grave escalation” that poses a serious threat to regional security, in a post on X.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the latest strike and said “attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law,” also writing on X.

The civil war in Yemen flared up once again this summer and significantly intensified last month, after years of relative calm.

In retaliation for a Saudi blockade on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, the Houthis announced in July they would target Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, and began a campaign of missile attacks against Saudi infrastructure, including oil refineries.

Last month, they conducted a lightning offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, capturing the port of Mocha and closing in on Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.

That led the Saudi-backed Yemeni government based in Aden to launch a major offensive, but it has struggled to retake much ground.

Saudi Arabia has for 11 years tried to contain the conflict on its southern border through military force and diplomacy – first waging war with the Houthis, then pursuing peace talks with them and restoring diplomatic talks with their backer, Tehran.

Despite the efforts, a series of miscalculations has left Riyadh exposed to further conflict in Yemen, experts say.

Saudi Arabia ended its longstanding partnership with the UAE late last year over its backing of a rival force in Yemen, misjudged Trump’s willingness to back it if it needed support, and struggled to organize disintegrated armed factions fighting the Houthis.

The escalation threatens Saudi Arabia’s broader ambitions to become an international destination for business and tourism.

On Sunday, the Saudi energy ministry said the World Petroleum Congress began as scheduled in Riyadh, but it’s unclear how many delegates are attending.

CNN’s Ibrahim Dahman, Michael Williams and Mostafa Salem contributed reporting.

title: Fixated on AI, the world has forgotten what is staring it in the face: nuclear annihilation | Simon Tisdall
description:
This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day
Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn.
fullText:
This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing ‘end times’ closer by the day

Humankind has fearfully and sometimes joyfully anticipated the end of the world ever since it began. The Bible’s Book of Revelation speaks of “end times”, a period of tribulation, war, famine, plague, floods and environmental catastrophe that may seem a less absurd prospect today than perhaps it once did. Islam, too, posits a fateful day of judgment or day of reckoning. Christian evangelicals believe that, in the final rapture, a chosen few – the righteous or the “elect” – will be saved while sinners burn. It’s a minority view. Matthew’s gospel predicts most people will defy, ignore or ridicule warnings of imminent Armageddon. Peter, another of Jesus’s disciples, agreed: “In the last days, scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.” Yet such worldly scepticism does not mean a universal cataclysm is less likely. It may make it more probable.

Donald Trump’s blanket denials of the dangers ostensibly posed by artificial intelligence, whose uncontrolled development is seen by some as the latest harbinger of apocalypse, could be interpreted as fulfilling Peter’s prophecy. This US president, the nearest thing the world has to a one-man doomsday machine, is a great one for scoffing and evil desires. In Robert Harris’s 2019 novel, The Second Sleep, a worried scientist lists half a dozen ways the world might end. They include devastating climate change, pandemic disease, a giant asteroid collision with Earth, or some other overwhelming calamity. Few heed the fictional scientist’s fears. In the event, what destroys him and almost everybody else is a disturbingly plausible cyber crash – a global digital and internet meltdown.

While arguments rage over whether large language models will acquire consciousness and moral agency – and the power to delete humanity – existential AI threats remain, as of now, open to mitigation. In sharp contrast, extraordinary complacency surrounds the most pressing, avoidable and proven human-made threat to life on Earth. It is as if the world has been seized by collective deafness and by a blind refusal to see what’s staring it in the face. This is no scoffing matter. The accelerating, global proliferation of advanced nuclear weapons is bringing real-time “end times” closer to home by the day. The question increasingly is not “if” but “when” limited or full-scale nuclear warfare will erupt. Eighty-one years after Hiroshima, how much longer can our luck hold?

Alarm bells are ringing, if only people would listen. Desperate Vladimir Putin recently threatened to deploy Russia’s entire nuclear arsenal, comprising about 4,400 warheads, against Nato countries if they activated a supposed plan to invade the Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad. He offered no evidence for his claim, and it’s true that the frequent Kremlin nuclear sabre-rattling since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine went pear-shaped has diminished Moscow’s credibility. Yet that in itself is destabilising. To work, nuclear deterrence relies on an adversary believing the threat is real. Disbelief invites miscalculation. At the same time, Putin’s inability to halt Ukraine’s conventional drone and missile attacks deep inside Russia may be edging him closer to pressing the nuclear button, possibly in the form of low-yield tactical or “battlefield” nukes.

Trump’s bottom-line justification for the illegal US-Israel war on Iran is his wilfully mendacious claim that Tehran was weeks away from obtaining the bomb. He claims to be protecting the world from nuclear war. Yet his reckless threat, issued at the UN, to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” implies a possible US nuclear attack. Trump’s hypocrisy is stunning. The US is upgrading its nuclear arsenal of 3,700 warheads and may resume nuclear tests. It unreservedly supports Israel’s hidden nuclear weapons programme. And Trump is pursuing a lucrative deal with Saudi Arabia, another bitter foe of Iran, to provide civilian nuclear technology that he knows could be repurposed to make weapons. That has prompted regional countries such as Turkey and Egypt to consider going nuclear.

Similarly perilous trends are evident across Asia. North Korea’s great panjandrum, Kim Jong-un, has succeeded in gaining de facto international acceptance of his country’s status as a nuclear weapons state. South Korea said in August that Pyongyang now possesses up to 120 warheads – which Kim brandishes to intimidate neighbours. All but discarded are the twin principles that underpinned the west’s postwar Korea policy: reunification and denuclearisation. Heedless of first-term humiliations, Trump is again seeking a summit with Kim, whom he bizarrely terms a friend. “As long as I’m around, he [Kim] is going to be fine,” he boasted. Japan and South Korea don’t share his confidence. Both debate acquiring nuclear weapons in self-defence. Meanwhile, China’s president, Xi Jinping, having again bamboozled a fawning Trump at their Washington summit, is reportedly building nukes like there’s no tomorrow – which, at this rate, there may not be.

Addressing the UN general assembly, secretary-general António Guterres warned the world has reached “the most dangerous nuclear moment” since 1989. Global military spending reached nearly $3tn last year, while AI is increasing uncertainty over nuclear command-and-control, the UN was told. Annual spending on nukes is up by 20%. In a new paper published by the non-partisan Arms Control Association (ACA), Daryl Kimball, the head of the ACA in Washington, bemoaned the absence of high-level disarmament talks between the main nuclear powers and the lapsing of strategic arms limitation treaties. “The nuclear sword of Damocles still hangs over all of us. The threat has become more complex, and in the absence of new arms-control breakthroughs, we are headed for an unprecedented three-way buildup of Chinese, Russian, and US nuclear forces,” Kimball warned.

The fragmentation of the rules-based international order provides aggravating context. Trump-era blasphemies – that might makes right, that international law and the non-proliferation treaty’s binding obligation to disarm can be ignored, and that the UN charter and human rights norms don’t apply to authoritarian “strongman” leaders – all grease the slide into nuclear anarchy. Unresolved forever wars in Palestine, Iran, Ukraine, Myanmar, Yemen and Sudan are base components of a third world war. Potentially earth-shattering, too, is the fast-developing contest for control of space, notably the race to build nuclear-powered lunar bases. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, under which more than 130 countries agreed the moon is no one’s property, is now routinely flouted by both governments and billionaires such as Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos. The weaponising of space by the US and others advances rapidly. Russia, for example, is reportedly developing an orbiting nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon.

If the human race really is determined to bring the heavens crashing down in a mad dash for eschatological self-destruction, this is the surest, quickest way to go about it. More surprising than the irresponsible behaviour of politicians is the deafening public silence, the absence of large-scale protest in much of the world, the complacency, bordering on indifference, that accompanies this global march to oblivion. If and when a final reckoning comes, individuals who stayed silent will be complicit in their own undoing. Hiroshima is not a shrine. It’s the future.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

fullText:
Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists

Humans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.

They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.

The experts behind The Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Health said all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.

“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.

To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).

“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”

Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, included air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition and climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict, declining overseas aid, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking and unhealthy ageing.

To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions.

Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.”

Action to limit global heating to about 1.8C (3.2F) rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat.

In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment.

Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announced large cuts to aid spending over the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition.

The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards.

The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems.

“We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”

description:
— The World Health Organization said Saturday it still doesn’t know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.
The U.N. health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. fullText:
GENEVA (AP) — The World Health Organization said Saturday it still doesn't know what caused the death of a young worker at a lab in Russia that focuses on plague and other illnesses.

The U.N. health agency has cited initial, unconfirmed reports suggesting pneumonic plague, a severe disease less common than the better-known bubonic plague linked to the Black Death in the Middle Ages. Pneumonic plague spreads from person to person, causing a severe form of pneumonia, but recovery rates are high if it is detected and treated in time.

WHO, in its first full Disease Outbreak News since the case emerged earlier this month, called for a continued investigation.

Russian health officials, it said, had conducted more than 5,500 tests and found no evidence of any dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.

"Additional clinical, epidemiological and laboratory information, including confirmation of the diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker, is required to improve confidence in the assessment," WHO said.

WHO continued to refer to "a purported second case" that, in emailed explanations to The Associated Press, it previously attributed to two tabloid news outlets in Britain and Serbia that cited unspecified reports in Russia.

Russia has denied any such second case.
