fullText:
Giant tortoises once pushed to the brink of extinction now outnumber humans in their home of the Seychelles, according to a new survey on one of the African nation’s most remote islands.

The survey, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter in the UK, estimated that about 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll, an Indian Ocean island group off the east coast of mainland Africa.

It is the highest figure ever recorded for the species, and far exceeds the human population of around 122,000 living in the tiny archipelago nation.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild. A much smaller population lives on Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands.

One of the world’s most undisturbed island ecosystems, Aldabra Atoll is home to several unique species that thrive in the remote haven.

The species has rebounded from a dramatic decline. Heavy exploitation during the 19th century reduced its population on the island to fewer than 1,000, pushing the species to the brink of extinction.

A recovery program helped secure strict nature reserve status for the atoll in 1981. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site a year later, giving the population room to rebound.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said in a statement.

“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

Creating the new estimate required more than just a headcount. The figures are based on an analysis of five years of tortoise counts conducted between 2018 and 2022, and is the first update since a widely cited estimate of 100,000 tortoises in the late 1990s.

“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

Bunbury added the team of scientists on the study have produced the most reliable baseline for the species, which can be used as a benchmark to track its population for decades to come.

Despite the encouraging population estimate, the study’s authors said continued vigilance is crucial as the climate crisis brings longer and more frequent droughts that could reduce shade and food for the tortoises. Rising sea levels as the planet warms also threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitat.

The world’s oldest known tortoise, a 194-year-old called Jonathan, is likely to have come from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles.

Guinness World Records lists Jonathan as the oldest living land animal and the oldest tortoise ever. He was believed to be about 50 years old when he was moved to the British Overseas Territory of St. Helena in 1882.

title: Former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
description:
— Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.
Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S.
fullText:
OSLO, Norway (AP) — Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former U.N. human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.

Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to U.S. President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of the U.N. commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.

Pillay's work "is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world," said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, in announcing her win in Oslo, Norway, as part of the peace prize's 125th anniversary.

The Norwegian committee said it sought to strengthen international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay's award was a message to those seeking to undermine "the international rules-based system and the institutions."

While her career has been global in scope, criticism often has been fiercely local, notably in places like Israel and in apartheid-era South Africa as she and peers took on some of the world's most painful and sensitive legal issues and most vulnerable populations.

Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, the location of the trials of Nazi war criminals that helped lay the foundations of international law.

"Firstly, at this venue, your applause means a great deal to me," she said to a standing ovation. "You know, you don't want to receive an award, prize or anything unless the public agrees that you deserve this."

And, joking, she added: "But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information."

Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the U.N.-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.

Gaza was among Pillay's first comments Friday after hearing she had won. "What's happening there is genocide," she said in Germany, to more applause.

The commission last year also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defense minister "have incited the commission of genocide." Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.

Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of antisemitism or allegedly turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel. Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

In an interview with the AP last year, she recalled how she worked closely with some Jewish lawyers in the fight against apartheid in her native South Africa and was invited to Israel as the U.N. rights chief from 2008 to 2014.

The Nobel announcement came at another critical time for Gaza, just two days after the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, that killed about 1,200 people and sparked the war. Over 74,000 Palestinians have since been killed, with their territory devastated. Saturday marks a year since a fragile ceasefire took effect, while Israeli strikes continue.

A senior Hamas official, Bassem Naim, in a statement Friday called the Nobel for Pillay a message of hope for Palestinians, especially in Gaza, that "humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice."

The Israeli foreign ministry, meanwhile, said in a statement that "if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn't just be a contender. She'd be a frontrunner."

It added on X that the award "isn't a recognition of justice. It's the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice."

The award also was announced less than three weeks before Israel's election, in which Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power. For Israelis, however, the issue is less about the government's approach to Gaza and more about how well it would protect them from further attacks.

Pillay's win brings renewed attention to Trump's ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court, where Pillay was a judge from 2003 to 2008. The Trump administration already has sanctioned 13 of the ICC's staff members, among them key prosecutors and nine judges including the court's Japanese President Tomoko Akane.

In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump called the court an "out of control institution" and an "anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction" over the U.S. as he urged member states to quit the "rogue institution immediately."

There are fears the court as a whole could be sanctioned, a move that could seriously hamper its ability to mete out justice.

Pillay is currently serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, the highest court of the United Nations, in the ongoing genocide case against Myanmar.

When countries do not have a national on the court's permanent, 15-judge panel, they can appoint an expert of their choice. Gambia, which launched the proceedings in 2019, selected Pillay when the country accused Myanmar of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority group.

As a young lawyer in apartheid South Africa, part of Pillay's work involved establishing key rights for political prisoners being held on Robben Island, which included Mandela, who later won the Nobel Peace Prize.

After apartheid ended, then-South African President Mandela appointed Pillay to be the country's first non-white woman to serve as a High Court judge.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year's prize, with just over a quarter of them organizations.

Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation.

Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.

In Trump's second term, he has been outspoken about his desire for the Nobel, but has expressed doubts that the committee would ever award him the prize.

"They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me," Trump told reporters Wednesday.

Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.

Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week, in the categories of medicine, physics, chemistry and literature. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Dazio reported from Berlin and Keaten from Geneva. Associated Press journalists Gerald Imray in Cape Town, South Africa, Ali Swenson in New York, Cara Anna in Jerusalem, Molly Quell and Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands, and Mark Lewis in Stavanger, Norway, contributed to this report.

title: Wales captain James has World Cup on her mind
description: Wales take on Albania over two legs in the semi-finals of the play-offs motivated by reaching a World Cup for the first time.
fullText:
Captain Angharad James says the Women's World Cup is always on her mind as Wales prepare for Friday's play-off semi-final first leg in Albania.

Wales' women look to take a step closer to a first World Cup appearance in the nation's history as they face the Albanians in Shkoder.

Rhian Wilkinson's side will have home advantage in next Tuesday's return leg at Parc y Scarlets with the winners facing either Norway or Romania in a two-legged play-off final in December.

Even if they come through both play-off rounds, Wales may then have to negotiate inter-confederation play-offs in February to book their place at next year's tournament in Brazil.

Yet James, 32, says she is already thinking about the idea of representing Wales at the World Cup during "every training session, every day".

"It's always in the back of my mind," the Seattle Reign midfielder added.

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

"I've always wanted to play in a World Cup and I think if you ask the majority of the group, the way we turn up and train and play every day for [our] club is for moments like this with our national team.

"Every day I'll make sure I do extras. I do everything that I can to best prepare myself and the team to reach the first World Cup."

James was a central part of the squad who ended Wales' wait for a women's major championship appearance by qualifying for Euro 2025.

As they look to make it two tournaments in succession, Wilkinson's players did all they could during the group stage of World Cup qualifying by topping Group B4.

But with no automatic qualification route available to teams in League B, Wales face a demanding play-off process which begins in Albania.

Even with their squad depleted by injury, Wales will expect to overcome the Albanians, who they beat twice in the group phase.

But a probable play-off final against Norway – with the second leg away from home – would be a far sterner challenge.

Even so, James says Wales have the "strength and depth" required to carry them to a World Cup.

"We know it's not an easy road ahead of us," she added.

"It's a big challenge. We've got a big game [in Albania], we've got big games ahead of us and the road is never easy.

"But it's one that I truly believe this group can get through. With the help of the staff and the whole squad, we can achieve big things and reaching the World Cup would be the biggest honour."

Wales eye shutout in World Cup play-off first leg

Wales focus on Albania as Grainger reunion looms

Wales' injury worries deepen as duo withdraw

Should they overcome Albania – and Norway beat Romania - Wales will turn their attention to a reunion with Gemma Grainger.

The Englishwoman, who came close to guiding Wales to the 2023 World Cup, stepped down as Welsh boss in January 2024 to take charge of Norway.

Upsetting Grainger's Norway, who are ranked 14th in the world, would be a major coup for Wales – and yet at this stage, Wilkinson's squad do not know if that would be enough to seal a World Cup place.

There will be eight European play-off winners, with seven progressing straight to Brazil and one – the lowest-ranked nation from the group stage of qualifying – going into inter-confederation play-offs next February.

"So as players, do you celebrate that moment, do you not? It's mixed emotions, but hopefully the pathway will change in the near future."

title: Mourinho calls criticism of Mbappe 'ridiculous'
description: Jose Mourinho defends Kylian Mbappe who has been scrutinised during the international break.
fullText:
Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho has defended Kylian Mbappe over his activities during the international break - describing criticism as "ridiculous".

France captain Mbappe withdrew from international duty after picking up an injury against Turkey on 25 September.

He later shared images on social media at a Paris Fashion Week event and also riding a bicycle - something Mourinho had previously said was against his rules.

"When it comes to Real Madrid, it's always different," he said.

"But all the players did exactly what they were supposed to during the break. And then you always want to look for more problems and issues.

"What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to and when he fails at that and he stops being a Real Madrid player for 24 hours, you will not see that player on the bench because he will be at home."

He said an image of Mbappe riding a bike in Switzerland had been misrepresented, saying that bicycles were available for guests at his hotel complex to use for short journeys.

Asked if coverage of Mbappe was exaggerated he added: "Exaggerated, no - I think it was ridiculous.

"If Mbappe plays tomorrow, it's because he hasn't failed Real Madrid and he hasn't failed to fulfil his obligations to the club," he added.

Real are six points behind leaders Barcelona in the La Liga table after seven games.

Mbappe, 27, is one of the favourites to win this year's Ballon d'Or. He scored 42 goals in 44 games for his club last season but they did not win any trophies.

He won the World Cup Golden Boot with 10 goals, taking his career tally at World Cups to a record 22 - although France finished fourth.

title: Rangers boss McInnes 'not a fan' of extended break
description: Rangers manager Derek McInnes says he is "not a fan" of the extended international break which he considers "too long".
fullText:
Rangers manager Derek McInnes says he is "not a fan" of the extended international break which he considers "too long".

The Ibrox club had 13 players away on duty for their countries after the Scottish Premiership win over Celtic on 20 September.

McInnes says the full squad will only train together on Friday, the day before the visit of Kilmarnock and 19 days after their derby triumph.

"Our players are away with different federations, working with different staff and travelling all over the world for four games," McInnes said.

"It's tough for the players to be away from their families, but equally for us there is a lot of nervousness about your players going into other countries' hands for so long.

"They're all back in today but they're not all training. So by the time we get on to the pitch together tomorrow it'll be 19 days since the Celtic game.

"That's longer than a lot of tournaments for a lot of countries. I know it's set in stone - but I'm not a fan of it to be honest."

Shankland sure lots of games to come by return

Why early-season data points to Premiership style shift

Rangers went into the break on a run of six straight victories, the latest two over Celtic in the League Cup and Premiership.

It was a much-needed revival for McInnes, who was named the Premiership manager of the month for September, and his side after a rocky start to his time at Ibrox which involved an exit from European competition.

The Rangers boss says he is under "no illusions" their good form has to continue, and also revealed he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at the club's training ground.

The former Manchester United boss was a regular visitor to Tynecastle last season as McInnes spearheaded Hearts' unexpected title charge.

"He spent a bit of time with the staff and me, chewing the fat as he does," McInnes explained. "He has always been really supportive, and I'm sure he is with a lot of managers.

"I've had a couple of conversations with him since I've been at the club, but to see him in person was good. Particularly after his health scare.

"He enjoyed what we were doing at Hearts and he was a regular visitor. But he understood the opportunity for me to come here was there and we spoke long and hard about that.

"He spoke about his own difficult starts at Man United, and he said it's how you finish a campaign not how you start the campaign. Sometimes it can take time.

"He thought we were really strong on the performance at Celtic Park in particular."

title: Wales target clean sheet in World Cup play-off first leg
description: Rhian Wilkinson makes a clean sheet the first target for Wales in Friday's Women's World Cup play-off semi-final first leg against Albania.
fullText:
Rhian Wilkinson has identified a clean sheet as the first target for Wales in Friday's Women's World Cup play-off semi-final first leg against Albania.

Wales face Albania at the 16,000-capacity Loro Borici Stadium in Shkoder before next Tuesday's return in Llanelli.

Wilkinson's side beat their play-off opponents twice during the group stage of World Cup qualifying in April, when they followed up a 4-0 home victory with a scrappy 1-0 success on their travels.

Wales have not been helped by a string of injuries as they prepare for another double-header against Albania.

When asked what would represent a positive first leg for Wales, Wilkinson said: "I'll stick with a clean sheet and a strong performance."

She added: "I think what I would say is that this is home and away, back-to-back play-off and we've had some experiences with this.

"We continue to grow through those and it's about taking care of delivering a performance away and then making sure we come home and deliver another one in the next few days."

Women's World Cup qualifying play-off semi-final

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC Two Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales Extra, Radio Cymru, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Wales are without nine regular members of their squad for the next stage of their bid to reach a first World Cup.

Olivia Clark, Poppy Soper, Rhiannon Roberts, Hayley Ladd, Ella Powell, Laura Hughes, Mia Ross, Ffion Morgan and Ceri Holland - who has been Wales' most influential performer since the retirement of Jess Fishlock - are all absent through injury.

Aside from back-up keeper Soper, all those players would have been contenders to play some part in the two Albania ties.

The long list of absentees means there is a youthful look to Wales' squad, with six uncapped players and a number of others with minimal international experience involved.

Nevertheless, Wilkinson says Wales are well placed to cope thanks to their regular policy of inviting young players to train with her senior side.

"I think it would be silly for me to say that having nine injuries was predictable - I think that was out of the norm," Wilkinson said.

"If I could have had no injuries I would have, but equally this is football and we adapt and we are a small country.

"I don't think we can pretend that we have unlimited players, so the fact I'm able to put together a team of 23 that has such strength and with a lot of experience is a good thing."

Goalkeepers Soffia Kelly and Lucy Farrell-Shrouder, centre-back Cadi Rodgers, wide player Heidi Hills and forwards Casi Gregson and Olivia Francis are the six players with Wales in Albania who are yet to be capped.

Then there are the likes of Scarlett Hill, Phoebie Poole, Tianna Teisar and Chloe Williams who have only a handful of international appearances between them.

Wilkinson insists the various inexperienced players are "absolutely" ready if required in what are high-stakes games.

"They've trained with a great intensity, they've done their work off the pitch and really involved themselves in meetings," she added.

"They've done everything they can to put themselves in the best possible position to get minutes."

Wales focus on Albania as Grainger reunion looms

Wales' injury worries deepen as duo withdraw

Fishlock set for Wales return - but not as player

Wales topped their qualifying group courtesy of a rousing home win over the Czech Republic in the final game of that stage in June.

As well as cruising to victory over Albania, in Wrexham, they thumped Montenegro in their home group fixture.

Yet Wales' away form was nowhere near as convincing, with draws against the Czechs and in Montenegro either side of their triumph in Albania.

The Albanians are ranked 68th in the world, 37 places below Wales, but Wilkinson expects another stern examination against "a team that really knows what their strengths are".

"I think we I've spoken quite honestly [about how in] the second group game against them, they definitely could have scored at least once or twice," she added.

"I expect it to be a resilient performance from both teams, to stick in it and try to bring our best versions of ourselves. They give everything for their badge like we will for ours, so it'll be a tough match."

The prize on offer against Albania is a two-legged World Cup play-off final against either Norway or Romania in early December.

If they get that far, Wales would start as underdogs against Gemma Grainger's Norway side.

At this stage, Wales do not know if wins over Albania and Norway would be enough to seal a World Cup place.

There will be eight European play-off winners, with seven progressing straight to Brazil and one – the lowest-ranked nation from the group stage of qualifying – going into inter-confederation play-offs next February.

When asked whether the play-off process should be simpler, Wilkinson said: "This is above my pay grade. What I will say is it doesn't help to get stuck in what could be or what comes afterwards.

"There's different scenarios here, but it's not for us to change that.

"For right now, this is our path and we'll just keep taking care of what's in front of us one step at a time."

"I've had a couple of conversations with him since I've been at the club, but to see him in person was good. Particularly after his health scare.

"He enjoyed what we were doing at Hearts and he was a regular visitor. But he understood the opportunity for me to come here was there and we spoke long and hard about that.

"He spoke about his own difficult starts at Man United, and he said it's how you finish a campaign not how you start the campaign. Sometimes it can take time.

"He thought we were really strong on the performance at Celtic Park in particular."

title: Trump Tourism Effects
description:
In the past day or two on social media I kept seeing this graph from a Semafor story on the declining volume of international visitors to the United States.
Semafor Graph.
It seems to show, and was being remarked on as showing, that the second Trump administration has been responsible for a drop in visitors from abroad from some countries on a scale comparable to the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. My first thought was “that can’t be true”. And indeed it is not true.
fullText:
In the past day or two on social media I kept seeing this graph from a Semafor story on the declining volume of international visitors to the United States.

It seems to show, and was being remarked on as showing, that the second Trump administration has been responsible for a drop in visitors from abroad from some countries on a scale comparable to the effects of the Covid-19 pandemic. My first thought was “that can’t be true”. And indeed it is not true. I mean, the pandemic shut down air travel almost completely for a while. The current administration’s actions have been terrible in many ways and led to direct, negative consequences for tourism, too. But they haven’t been on that scale. Something’s wrong with the graph.

These numbers come from International Trade Administration’s I-94 arrivals data. They maintain a spreadsheet that counts all international visitors by country of residence who arrive in the U.S., spend at least one night here, are among qualified visa holders, including tourist visas and waivers and so forth. This is a monthly series. Right now, we only have data up to August of 2026, and for a couple of countries in the graph only up till June. I think—I am only guessing—that what the person who made this graph did was aggregate to yearly totals, plot those points, and then smooth them. (That’s why the y-axis values are so large in comparison to the ones on the monthly graphs I’m about to show you.) But the data for 2026 are only for half the year, hence the giant drop.

I went and got the data myself and took a look at it. Here’s the raw monthly series for the same countries as in the one above:

It’s noisy because tourism is highly seasonal. Even so, the catastrophic effects of the pandemic are obvious, as is the fact that whatever is going on in the past year isn’t nearly as severe as that. Though something is going on. We can smooth the monthly data directly by calculating a trailing average, which is just a moving average except the window we’re moving across the data doesn’t extend beyond the current month. That way, we don’t illegitimately “look ahead” of the current month in a way that would make our moving average seem to anticipate the future. If we used an ordinary moving average it might seem like the trend was able to anticipate the Covid-19 downturn, for example. Here’s the result:

So, no Covid-scale drop. But still, not nothing. The Canadian dip, following the trade war Trump started for no good reason, is very substantial. Just eyeballing it, it seems about twice as large as the downturn that followed the global financial crisis of the Great Recession, which is quite remarkable. It also looks like French tourism has declined, but I’d need to look a little more closely at that series by itself, as it’s on quite a different scale.

The general lesson, I suppose, is just that it’s always worth trying to cultivate some sort of rough comparative sense of how big or small an effect you should be expecting to see in your data, so that when something goes wrong (as things so often do) you’re more likely to be brought up short by it.

Speaking of which, you might also wonder about the remarkable leap in visitors from Mexico around 2004-2005 that’s visible in both the original graph and my version of it. What happened there? The answer is not some sudden shift in tourism preferences, but our old friend, measurement change. Prior to 2005, visitors from Mexico originating within 25 miles of the border weren’t counted as visitors. After 2005, they were. Hence the jump. In a smaller but still noticeable way, data for 2014 aren’t fully comparable either, because overseas one-night-stay visitors were included that year. There is some documentation of this on this old BTS page. If you want to measure change, you can’t change the measure.

Update: Now that I have this data and am messing around with it, here’s one more. This is monthly data averaged with a 12-month trailing window, showing all travel to the U.S., broken out by different “regions”. Canada and Mexico are large enough to each be their own region. Looking at things this way deliberately smooths away all the seasonality. The size of the Canadian reaction to the Trump administration’s attack on them really is remarkable. Elbows up, Canada.

fullText:
Ukraine on Thursday accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest single attacks for weeks.

Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb.

The strikes come just a day after five children were among 22 killed when a Russian missile struck a five-storey apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernigiv region.

"The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians," Donetsk Governor Vadym Filashkin said, accusing Moscow of flouting "every conceivable rule of warfare and norm of international humanitarian law".

Kramatorsk City Council called it "yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".

"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it added.

There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian casualties in the conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.

Since Russia first invaded in 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.

The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war, but says the real number is considerably higher.

Last week, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had sanctioned massive attacks on civilian areas.

The Kremlin has denied the claim.

Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, has come under increasing attack, including on Wednesday when Russia launched a barrage of powerful ballistic and cruise missiles, and fast-moving, jet-powered drones.

The city's mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said two people were found dead on Thursday after a fire at a four-storey building that was hit by a drone in the densely populated Solomyansky district.

Klitschko has said the attacks, which have hit key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid, were "tearing Kyiv apart".

For the first few years of the war, Kyiv had been relatively spared from the devastation wrought on the frontline but should now be on a war footing, he argued.

Kramatorsk, which was home to some 150,000 people before the war, is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.

It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called "fortress belt" which troops are fighting to keep hold of.

Russian forces have edged close to the city's eastern fringes, which has prompted calls for the civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.

Filashkin said Thursday's strike, which happened at 10:00 am (0700 GMT), represented a "sharp deterioration" in security and ordered the suspension of public transport in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk.

"Under these circumstances, we cannot risk the lives of passengers and drivers," he said. "The safety of the residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is now our top priority."

Ukraine last month launched a counter-offensive against Russian troops around Lyman -- to the north of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk -- claiming some success in regaining pockets of territory.

fullText:
Béjar’s daughter was 14 when she told him Instagram was failing to keep her safe. So when he became part of Meta’s ‘wellbeing team’, he knew he had to speak out – and his testimony cost it billions

The Social Reckoning hits cinemas this Friday, but the real world has already been working on a sequel – or rather, a threequel. Directed by Aaron Sorkin, the movie is a follow-up to The Social Network, detailing the further misadventures of Mark Zuckerberg and his social media empire, and in particular Frances Haugen, the employee who in 2021 leaked internal documents that appeared to show Facebook was aware of the harms its products had inflicted.

It’s no spoiler to reveal the film climaxes with Haugen’s testimony to the US Senate, on 5 October 2021. That very same day, Arturo Béjar, a consultant on the wellbeing team of Instagram (which is also owned by Facebook), hit send on a long-gestating email to Zuckerberg and other senior Facebook executives on a similar theme. “I wanted to bring to your attention what I believe is a critical gap in how we as a company approach harm, and how the people we serve experience it,” Béjar began, before laying out some shocking statistics from his team’s survey. For example: 24.4% of 13-15-year-olds on Instagram said they had received unwanted advances, and 21.8% said they had been the target of bullying on the platform in the past seven days. Furthermore, 51% of Instagram users said they had had a bad or harmful experience in the past seven days. Only 1% of them reported it, and of those, 2% had the content taken down – so just 0.02%. This was a far greater degree of harm than the company’s existing measurements suggested. Zuckerberg never replied.

Béjar has seen The Social Reckoning, and he recognises Jeremy Strong’s portrayal of Zuckerberg as a detached, awkward, humourless control freak all too well. “Oh, it’s accurate,” he says. “I don’t recall him ever being empathetic to the harm that somebody was experiencing and wanting to make that better … The only thing that really consistently came across in all my interactions with him was winning. He’s one of the most fiercely competitive people I know.”

One time, Béjar recalls, he and Zuckerberg were walking together after a fraught meeting. “One of the things that I used to say when bad things were happening is, ‘Are we having fun yet?’ Just as a little kind of defusing humour thing,” says Béjar. “And he looked at me, very intense, and said, ‘I’m not here for fun – I’m here for impact.’ That was my experience of him, over and over and over again.”

That 2021 email was the beginning of the end for Béjar. He was still hoping Zuckerberg would respond to his appeal to engineer a “culture shift” in the way Instagram dealt with protecting its young users. The next day, however, Zuckerberg issued a statement to Facebook employees about Haugen’s testimony and the leaked “Facebook Files” that were being reported by the Wall Street Journal and others. “At the heart of these accusations is this idea that we prioritise profit over safety and wellbeing. That’s just not true,” Zuckerberg wrote. But by then Béjar knew it was true.

In many respects Béjar is the perfect witness: sincere, calmly spoken, emotionally literate, able to express complex ideas in accessible ways, and possessing reams of inside knowledge. He’s seemingly the opposite of Zuckerberg. At times during our conversation, as we sit outside a cafe in north London, he has to pause mid-sentence, his eyes welling with tears. He apologises afterwards for getting emotional, but that seems to be exactly what these issues demand.

There’s another reason Béjar has been such a powerful spokesperson: he has a direct connection to the issues, via his teenage daughter. When she was in her early teens, in about 2018, she told him she regularly received sexist comments and unsolicited nude photos from men via her Instagram account. Her female friends experienced the same thing. There was no point reporting it, she told him, because it never resulted in any meaningful action. Commenters might get blocked – after which they would simply open a new account under a different name – or Instagram would judge that the behaviour didn’t violate their policies.

Until that point, like many early Facebook employees, Béjar believed he was making the world a better place. When he started in 2009, the company was booming and the idealism was infectious. “The promise was, we’ll create something that keeps you close to your friends. I think a lot of people back then believed in that. And that’s not what they built.”

Béjar, 55, was an early tech enthusiast. Born in Mexico City, the son of a doctor father and an artist mother, he taught himself to code and blagged his way into a job with IBM when he was 15. He came to Silicon Valley, after a spell in London, in 1993, and worked at Yahoo for 11 years before he joined Facebook.

As senior engineering and product leader at Facebook, Béjar was responsible for security but also for customer care: “developing tools that help people learn to be with each other online” – especially young people. For example, he developed a more nuanced way for young people to report content they didn’t like. If the button on Facebook said “report”, teens tended not to use it, but if it was changed to “I don’t want to see this”, three times as many teens would click on it. And if you could grade the intensity of that feeling, from “mildly annoying” to “really bad”, that made it easier to deal with problems.

“Most people who behave aggressively online, if you give them private, respectful feedback, they’re like, ‘Oh sorry, I didn’t mean to,’” Béjar says. “And that’s how we work as a society, right?” He gestures to the pedestrian street around us; people are peacefully going about their business. “What makes this street nice is not that there’s police everywhere enforcing our behaviour, it’s that we have all these ways where we signal to each other what it’s like to be safe, even though you might have fundamentally different values.” He built more than a dozen Facebook products on that premise, he says, with extraordinary results. “Basically, half the people change behaviour the first time you go, like, ‘Yeah, we don’t do that here.’”

He left the company, amicably, in 2015 because he was going through a divorce and wanted to spend more time with his young son and daughter. By the time he found out about his daughter’s Instagram experience, other young victims of social media were becoming known. In 2017, 14-year-old Molly Russell died from an act of self-harm in her London bedroom. The coroner’s report said her depression was exacerbated by her social media consumption, especially Instagram. Wider issues with Facebook were also beginning to emerge: its role in election manipulation, stoking ethnic violence, promoting inflammatory posts.

After raising his concerns with the company, Béjar was invited to return in 2019, on a two-year contract as a consultant on Instagram’s “wellbeing” team. “I still believed that the reason the stuff that was happening to my daughter and all her friends, and every other kid I’ve talked to since, was because as companies get big, sometimes the general doesn’t know what the soldiers are doing. That was my thesis for almost all the time I was there: Mark doesn’t know … and if he knew, he would fix it.”

Evidence to the contrary started piling up, though. “What I started finding when I came back is that they did know. They knew about addiction, they knew how bad it was. They knew about Molly Russell.” It later emerged that Facebook had internal research confirming Instagram’s negative effects on teenage mental health, but had kept it secret. The wellbeing team could not get anything done, Béjar says. “They could dream up a good product that would make things better, and they couldn’t get it out the door. You would put it through the review process and all the teams that would review it would just kill parts of it until there was nothing left.”

The ethos had changed, he says. For all the talk about connecting the world and bringing people together, the priority was simply growth, it seemed: attracting more users and keeping them on the platform for as long as possible. Video content was now set to autoplay; notifications were frequent, as were suggestions of other people to follow; “infinite scroll” algorithmically served up content tailored to users’ continuously tracked habits. All the customer care tools Béjar had previously developed – such as the “I don’t want to see this” button – had gone.

Béjar’s team developed a tool aimed at people with a history of posting comments that got reported and deleted – “the worst of the worst” – so that when they posted something inflammatory, they would get a community note telling them: “You might want to phrase this differently.” “We were in the process of getting that approved. And one of the people in the review meeting said, ‘What if 50 Cent gets this thing and makes fun of it? We can’t have that.’ That was the driver.”

The anecdote chimes with Facebook’s secretive “cross-check” system, revealed in the Facebook Files, where posts by celebrities, politicians and other high-profile “business partners” were moderated more leniently, even if they violated the company’s stated policies.

Had he known what he knows now, Béjar would never have allowed his daughter on Instagram in the first place, he says. “Instagram is built on three pillars: addictive design, connecting you to strangers, and rewarding you for doing things that are exhibitionistic, performative or aggressive,” he says. None of these are safe or desirable for young people, most people would agree. He compares social media to the tobacco industry: “This is the equivalent of handing your kids a cigarette and being like, ‘Hey, you’ll be cooler if you smoke.’” On unwanted sexual advances, he says, “What Instagram is effectively doing is, while your kid is in the bedroom, it’s lining up strangers outside the window and inviting them in.”

Béjar believes that the tone is squarely set by Zuckerberg, as the longtime CEO, chair and controlling shareholder of Meta: “If Mark woke up tomorrow and was like, ‘I want to create something that’s genuinely good for kids,’ it would take the company six months to fundamentally shift all these things and drive all these harms down. They have the technology, they have the people, they have the expertise, they have the infrastructure. It’s his refusal to do that which creates a culture.”

Ultimately, Béjar faced the same dilemma Haugen did. Speaking out meant ending his career, as well as being ostracised from his colleagues and his community. But, he says, “You have to ask yourself: who am I protecting? Am I protecting the company or my way of life or my being? Or am I protecting other people? It took me years, to really walk away from the identity that I had developed when I was working there.” He was emboldened by Haugen’s courageous example and by the treatment she received afterwards: “Internally, they would call her ‘the leaker’. They wouldn’t say her name.”

When approached for comment, a Meta spokesperson said: “We all share a common goal of providing safe, meaningful online experiences for young people. Our record shows that we’ve spent the past decade researching and developing numerous tools and resources to support teens and empower parents, including Teen Accounts, which place teens in protective settings by default. We’ll continue to make improvements and partner with parents and experts to keep teens safe.” Meta has repeatedly rejected implications that engagement stands in contrast to its commitment to teen safety.

Despite its best efforts to contrive a triumphant finale, The Social Reckoning ends on a bit of a sour note. There was no real reckoning for Meta. Donald Trump was re-elected; social media companies forgot about their commitment to fact-checking, Meta included. And Zuckerberg’s company continues to grow and profit from the digital economy – including the AI economy. Last month, still reeling from the reaction to Meta’s camera-enabled “pervert glasses”, Zuckerberg unveiled Muse, Meta’s cute and cuddly AI agent, which can perform personalised tasks such as shopping or sending emails. Even Haugen herself recently admitted: “We are worse off today than when I leaked the Facebook documents.”

Had they waited until this month, the film-makers might have been able to craft a happier ending. The landmark trial brought by multiple US states in August ended two days after Béjar’s testimony. Meta abandoned their challenge and settled the case (denying any wrongdoing). The company will have to pay out up to $18bn (£13.6bn); it’s a relatively small sum, considering that Meta’s revenue in 2025 was more than $200bn (£151.5bn). More significantly, for the first time, the company agreed to major changes to protect teens: two-hour daily time limits for under-18s across Instagram and Facebook; blocking notifications during school hours; blocking the apps at night; turning off autoplay; giving parents greater control; and other safety features.

“I think it’s an extraordinary accomplishment,” says Béjar. “Nobody else in the world has got them to agree that they will reduce the hours kids spend on the platform. Or that they’re going to be more transparent about how they assess age, or that it will reduce home notifications.”

These measures won’t fix everything, but they’re progress. Meta lost another trial, brought by the US state of New Mexico in March, again over misleading the public about safety, and had to pay $942m (£713.7m) in fines and damages. There are dozens more cases in the pipeline. Governmental regulation is tightening around the world. Perhaps the tide is turning.

If it is, it will be some relief to Béjar. He has spent much of the past three years campaigning, testifying, talking to governments, academics, regulators. He has other interests beyond the tech world. Even as he was quitting Meta, he was writing the libretto for a musical collaboration with the composer Philip Glass. He is writing an opera based on Charles Darwin’s theory of emotion in animals, with the British composer Jocelyn Pook. His daughter, by the way, now earns her living restoring classic sports cars.

There’s still work to be done. What’s really needed, Béjar argues, is independent assessment and comparison of the safety of social media sites – the same way we monitor, say, vehicle emissions. “Every parent and every kid deserves to know: what is the likelihood that this bad thing is going to happen to you on any of these services?” But at last it feels like things are headed in that direction, he says. “It’s still just the beginning, but I do feel hope.”

title: Evans to defend title in extended WRC calendar including Scotland
description: The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place in October as the 2027 World Rally Championship comes to the BBC.
fullText:
The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place from 3-7 October in an extended 2027 World Rally Championship (WRC) calendar released by the FIA and the sport's promoters.

The gravel event in Aberdeenshire will form the 12th round of a 15-event calendar, as it joins the USA as new events on the schedule.

It is the first time the United Kingdom has hosted a round of the WRC since 2019, and BBC Sport will provide extensive live coverage of the rally.

It will also be a home round for new World Rally champion Elfyn Evans, who won the title in dramatic circumstances in Sardinia on Sunday after rival Oliver Solberg crashed at the end of the final stage.

In doing so, Evans became the first WRC champion from the UK in 25 years and joined the late Colin McRae and Richard Burns as the sport's top-level title winners.

Northern Ireland drivers Josh McErlean and Jon Armstrong also competed at the top level of the sport in 2026 and will be aiming to return next year.

In addition to Rally Scotland, the BBC's coverage will include five live stages plus the Power Stage on all WRC rounds, highlights programmes, plus digital clips and content across BBC platforms.

How Evans defied history to join rallying greats

Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC champion

The season will start on the icy tarmac roads in Monte Carlo from 21-24 January before rounds in the snow in Sweden and vast landscapes of Safari Rally Kenya.

Three tarmac events in a row then take place in Croatia, the Canary Islands and Japan, before the Acropolis Rally in Greece.

The WRC's Italian round moves from September to July, and will move from the gravel roads of Sardinia to tarmac in Rome.

The high-speed events in Estonia and Finland retain their back-to-back summer slots before the USA hosts its first WRC round in 39 years from 26-29 August.

The WRC last held a points-paying round in the USA at the Olympus Rally in 1988, and the championship will return as a gravel round after a successful candidate event in June.

Rally Scotland takes place in early October before a South American double-header, in Paraguay and Chile, and Rally Saudi Arabia round out the calendar.

The event in Saudi Arabia was set to end the 2026 season but it was cancelled due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Rally de Portugal will not feature in the 2027 calendar but is in talks to return in 2028.

The upcoming season will mark a new era of the sport with the introduction of a new promoter along with WRC27 regulations which will limit costs and reduce the horsepower of the top cars.

It will also mark the return of Ford as a manufacturer to the sport in a collaboration with the M-Sport banner.

2027 World Rally Championship calendar

Rallye Monte-Carlo 21-24 January

Acropolis Rally Greece 24-27 June

Rally Scotland 30 September-3 October

Rally del Paraguay 21-24 October

Rally Saudi Arabia 25-28 November

title: 'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil
description: Northern Ireland defenders Nat Johnson and Rebecca Holloway tell BBC Sport NI of their dream of reaching a first ever Women's World Cup as NI go through the play-offs.
fullText:
A World Cup staged in Brazil is the stuff of dreams for any footballer and the chance to experience that is on offer for Northern Ireland as they begin their play-off journey against Portugal with hope of securing a spot at next year's tournament.

It will be a difficult ask for Michael McArdle's side, which has been hit by a spate of injuries and features five new faces, but there is a quiet confidence in the group before what will be, for some of them, the biggest games in their careers to date.

First up, in what is set to be an arduous journey in search of a World Cup debut, is Friday's home leg at Inver Park (19:30 BST) against the Portuguese.

"When you're growing up, Brazil is the place to be, it's the home of football. It really doesn't get much better than that," said Norwich City defender Natalie Johnson.

"The fact that we are at this point and that it could be a reality, you don't need much more motivation than that.

"There's a lot on the line, but we are taking it one game at a time and I think if you look at it that way, nothing is impossible. Obviously there is that dream at the end of it, but we're focused on the game in front of us."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

As one of the lowest-ranked European sides in the play-offs, it is a difficult route to next summer's tournament for Northern Ireland.

If they overcome Portugal they will then face Croatia or Iceland in the next round. If they make it through those games, they will likely have an inter-continental play-off to make it the whole way to Brazil.

Portugal inflicted two defeats on in NI in Euro 2025 qualifying and sit 28 places higher in the Fifa world rankings, but Johnson and her side are not daunted by the task in front of them and instead want to embrace it.

"We absolutely believe these games are winnable," she added.

"We have a lot of experience in this team and the young players coming in bring their own individual experience and they really add to the squad. It's a good balance and we are going in to get something out of this.

"Any Portugal side is going to be very technical and we're expecting a very fast-paced game. We're going to have to be at our best to face that, quick football, and that's what we're working towards.

"On paper it might look like there is a big gap between the teams, but at the end of the day, it is a game of football and I think particularly on our home pitch it will be a much more level playing field."

Birmingham City defender Rebecca Holloway is one of the few survivors from the squad that qualified for Euro 2022, NI's first major tournament.

There have been a lot of changes to the squad since, but Holloway is excited for the future rather than dwelling on past achievements.

"It feels like a long time ago in a way, especially when you look at how much the squad has changed, but I think that's also what is very exciting," she said.

"It's like a new generation coming through and I think it's also important that we have some experienced players here to help those new faces. We're excited to see what they can do and encourage them to play with confidence and freedom and do what they are good at.

"We're slowly closing the gap on Portugal and the so-called bigger nations. They had a narrow 2-1 win over us at home in 2024 after a 4-0 away defeat, I think that shows that we are getting closer."

McArdle's youthful side do not have far to look for inspiration as to how to punch above their weight.

After assembling in camp on Monday, the team watched Northern Ireland's men's side 0-0 draw with Georgia.

That stalemate ensured Michael O'Neill's side stayed top of their Nations League group after picking up eight points from four games without conceding a goal.

"It was brilliant watching them play with such youth and energy and the exciting football that they are playing.

"This younger generation play with no fear and I think that is what the men's senior team are doing.

"I am hoping the young players see that and we can adopt the same attitude. I think we were all watching thinking we can't wait to do this on Friday."

title: How can home nations reach Women's World Cup?
description: England, Wales, Northern Ireland, Scotland and the Republic of Ireland are among those hoping to qualify for next year's Women's World Cup. What awaits them in the play-offs?
fullText:
England must get through two rounds of home and away ties to qualify for the Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Sarina Wiegman's European champions will play Greece in Crete in round one of the play-offs, with the first leg on Friday, 9 October at 17:30 BST.

The second leg will be played at home, at King Power Stadium in Leicester, on Tuesday, 13 October at 19:30 BST.

Commentary for both England matches will be on BBC Radio 5 Live.

Should England beat Greece over two games, they will face the winners of Slovakia v Ukraine, with the away fixture played first.

The exact dates of the potential second-leg fixtures are to be confirmed, although they will take place between 26 November and 5 December 2026.

England head coach Wiegman named her initial squad last month, with Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly notable absentees.

When asked why they were left out, Wiegman said: "They have not been playing to their full potential.

"Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us."

Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live: "That is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and, of course, they want to work on that."

All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup

Northern Ireland, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland are also involved in the play-offs as they chase World Cup places.

As with England, they are in action on Friday.

In round one, Wales face Albania at 17:00 BST - with coverage on BBC Two Wales from 16:45 BST.

Scotland play the Czech Republic at 18:00 BST, available to watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Alba.

Northern Ireland take on Portugal at 19:00 BST, available on BBC iPlayer.

The Republic of Ireland will play Kazakhstan at 12:00 BST.

Despite England securing five wins from their six qualifying matches, world champions Spain finished top of the Lionesses' group and secured the one automatic spot.

Wiegman said: "We knew what the play-offs would look like and, while we're pleased with the draw against Greece, the focus now is on making sure we're really well prepared.

"We want to dominate games and have a lot of the ball and that's something we will prepare for carefully."

England did not want to go through the play-offs but were given an unkind draw in the qualifying groups when they met world champions Spain.

However, Wiegman's side are in a strong position for the play-offs and will fancy their chances against Greece, who sit 55 places beneath them in the Fifa world rankings.

England also beat potential round two opponents Ukraine in both matches in the qualifying group stage, with an aggregate 9-1 score.

Northern Ireland face a tricky tie against a talented young squad from Portugal in round one. Portugal twice beat Northern Ireland in Euro 2025 qualifying.

Their task gets even harder if they make it through to round two, with potential opponents Iceland proving to be difficult to break down in their matches against England this year.

Scotland are hoping to reach just their second Women's World Cup finals, after a 2019 appearance. They failed to qualify in 2023 but have performed well this year, including drawing with Belgium, showing that they can compete with Europe's strongest teams.

They would need to produce their best in round two if they meet big-hitters Sweden, who have been semi-finalists in the past two Women's World Cups.

Wales have never beaten a top-20 ranked nation in a competitive fixture and are likely to need to do so to qualify.

There is optimism, though, as Rhian Wilkinson's side thrashed play-off opponents Albania 4-0 in their qualifying group.

Elsewhere, having performed superbly in qualifying, the Republic of Ireland have a tough play-off route with Belgium potentially waiting in round two.

First, Carla Ward's side will have to navigate a 3,100-mile trip to Kazakhstan, to tackle relatively unknown opposition.

title: She made India fall in love with women's cricket - now her era as captain is over
description: The skipper who led India to the historic 2025 World Cup win has stepped down from her role in all three formats.
fullText:
When Harmanpreet Kaur scored that unforgettable World Cup century against Australia in the 2017 semi-final, she not only changed the course of a match but the trajectory of women's cricket in India.

India went on to lose the final to England that year but women's cricket no longer remained a passing pursuit for the average Indian fan.

That dogged zeal to win she infused into the team helped them lift India's first women's World Cup trophy - the same feat that had eluded them in 2017 - in emphatic fashion eight years later.

Less than a year on, and within weeks of victories in the Asia Cup and the Asian Games, she has relinquished the captaincy, ending an era in which she became the team's most influential leader and one of the most recognisable figures in the sport.

Star opener Smriti Mandhana, her long-time deputy, has been appointed captain across all formats.

Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) secretary Devajit Saikia, coach Amol Muzumdar, Harmanpreet and Mandhana attended the review meeting at which the leadership change was ratified. The transition, however, was not entirely seamless.

Reports suggest the 37-year-old Harmanpreet was willing to relinquish the T20 captaincy immediately, but was keen to continue leading the side in One-Day Internationals and Tests so that younger players could benefit from her experience.

The BCCI, however, was intent on a younger person at the helm and opted for the 30-year-old Mandhana.

In some ways, the move mirrors the BCCI's decision to replace Suryakumar Yadav as captain of the men's T20 side shortly after India won the World Cup earlier this year, with the captaincy passing to Shreyas Iyer.

Harmanpreet's future as captain had become a subject of intense debate in cricketing circles after India's below-par performance at the T20 World Cup in England a few months ago.

Her own poor form with the bat amplified concerns and prompted the BCCI to consider changes that could help the team meet the growing challenges of a women's game that continues to expand rapidly around the world.

Approaching her 38th birthday, and after almost a decade at the helm, Harmanpreet found herself under increasing scrutiny as her form dipped.

Opinion on whether she should continue as captain was sharply divided among former women players and captains.

Former cricketer Diana Edulji, among the most respected names in the game, felt Harmanpreet had done everything that could reasonably have been expected of her and that it was time for a younger captain to take over. Former captain Anjum Chopra, meanwhile, argued that Harmanpreet's experience remained invaluable and that she should stay on.

Sensing that the BCCI was strongly inclined towards a change, Harmanpreet opted to step down during the review meeting. She later announced her decision in an emotional Instagram post.

"I feel I have done my duty. I gave this team everything I had," she wrote.

"Now, it is time for me to turn the page… Blood. Sweat. Sacrifice. Pride. I gave it all. Now, I'm ready to play for the love of the game again.

"Captaincy ends, the journey continues."

Harmanpreet's intention to continue playing now leaves the BCCI with another decision to make about her future.

In Suryakumar Yadav's case, he not only lost the captaincy but also his place in India's T20 side. Given the depth of talent available in the men's game, it was easier for Ajit Agarkar and his fellow selectors to take what was always likely to be a contentious decision.

The situation in the women's game is different. Despite Harmanpreet's modest recent form, replacing a player of her experience and stature may not be straightforward, as the talent pipeline is not yet as deep as it is in men's cricket.

Whatever the future holds, Harmanpreet has scripted among the more memorable careers in women's cricket. Spanning more than two decades, it is a journey marked by significant achievements and milestones.

Born into a family of modest means in Punjab's Moga city, Harmanpreet developed a passion for cricket at an early age.

Her family's support was vital in the early years, but her rise to national recognition came after she joined the Railways - a transition facilitated by Diana Edulji - and moved to Mumbai.

The superior facilities and greater professionalism associated with Mumbai's sporting culture helped accelerate her development.

She made her India debut in 2009 at the age of 20 and has remained an integral part of the national side across formats ever since.

An all-rounder for the better part of her first decade in cricket, she made herself indispensable to the side with her explosive middle-order batting, crafty off-spin and sharp fielding skills.

Her blistering century against Australia in the semi-final of the 2017 Women's ODI World Cup remains one of the defining knocks in the history of the women's game. India went on to lose to England in the final, but beating Australia was a monumental hurdle overcome.

That century also helped spark wider interest in women's cricket in India, and transformed Harmanpreet into a household name.

The second decade of her career showcased her prowess both as batter and captain. Having succeeded Mithali Raj as T20 captain in 2016, Harmanpreet assumed charge across all formats in 2022 and went on to guide India to some of the greatest successes in its history.

Her leadership was marked by an aggressive pursuit of victory. That fearless approach instilled confidence and ambition in her teammates, helping the team overcome even the previously unbeatable Australians, most memorably in the semi-final of the 2025 ODI World Cup.

Unlike in 2017, Harmanpreet couldn't get a hundred on that occasion, but her innings of 89 was a stellar effort as captain. Combined with Jemimah Rodrigues's century, it helped India secure a famous victory over their arch rivals.

India then defeated South Africa in the final to reach what many regard as the pinnacle of achievement in the history of Indian women's cricket.

With multiple titles and trophies won under her leadership, Harmanpreet leaves behind a formidable legacy for her successor, Smriti Mandhana, to emulate.

fullText:

England will host the Netball World Cup for the fourth time in 2031.

The quadrennial tournament will be held at Manchester's Co-op Live indoor arena, World Netball and England Netball announced on Thursday.

Liverpool staged the event when England last hosted in 2019.

World Netball president Liz Nicholl said: "After reviewing their strong bid, I am confident England Netball will host another thrilling international event, and I am excited to see what we can achieve together in 2031 and beyond."

Eastbourne put on the inaugural tournament in 1963, with Birmingham staging the 1995 edition.

England reached a World Cup final for the first time in 2023, but the Roses were denied a first title by 12-time winners Australia in Cape Town.

England also finished as runners-up in 1975, when the tournament was contested in a league format.

Baroness Sue Campbell, chair of England Netball, said: "To have the best netball players in the world coming to Manchester is a hugely exciting prospect, and I know the city will give them the welcome they deserve.

"This is a fantastic opportunity not only to showcase our sport on the biggest stage, but also to inspire the next generation of players and fans."

England Netball chief executive Fran Connolly said the tournament would provide "a powerful platform to grow the visibility, profile and impact of women's sport and netball across the UK".

The announcement comes in England Netball's centenary year.

title: Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending
description: As Lionel Messi's international career ends in fond farewell, Cristiano Ronaldo's is at risk of petering out. BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international career's of two football greats.
fullText:
On a night where one football legend received a grand farewell from his country, about 6,000 miles away, another released a lengthy statement discussing all the ways in which he had been wronged by his national team coach.

Argentina great Lionel Messi took the adulation of the crowd in Buenos Aires as his glittering international career ended with a goal against Benin on an emotional night.

Meanwhile, Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on social media, accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" while admitting he should be held accountable for his own actions.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.

Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado says "things will never be the same again" for Ronaldo and Portugal - so is this the beginning of the end?

Jesus has said the door is open for Ronaldo to return to the national team, but is it? Or will this saga continue, potentially closing the book on the international career of one of the greatest players of all time?

BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international careers of two football greats.

A rivalry that changed football

Watch: Rivals - Messi v Ronaldo

Listen: Sporting Giants - Messi v Ronaldo

The Ronaldo saga has been rumbling on for some time, with many fans critical of former Portugal boss Roberto Martinez's insistence on starting Ronaldo at this summer's World Cup.

At 41 years old, Ronaldo is not the dynamic player he once was and many suggested his presence hindered the team rather than helped.

However, things came to a head on Sunday when Ronaldo was an unused substitute in the Nations League win over Norway. The player subsequently left camp after finding out he would not start against Denmark in November.

On Tuesday, Ronaldo released an almost-2,000 word statement on Instagram in which he said Jesus had twice "broke his word" and accused him of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.

Ronaldo apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving the camp and said the consequences of that must be "assessed and punished" while also dismissing any suggestion that he had played his last match for Portugal.

"We will have one or more farewell matches, there will be time for that," the statement said.

Manager Jesus said on Sunday the door remains open for Ronaldo to return if he chooses to, but many are suggesting the damage is already done.

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring

Portuguese football journalist Delgado told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I don't think there is a way back. In the statement, Ronaldo says he will return to the national team but at the same time he calls Jesus a liar three times.

"In the polls in Portugal made about this issue, only 15% of the Portuguese were on Ronaldo's side and people think we owe him a lot but his time is already done and he must understand it.

"The problem is that Ronaldo does not understand it, he wants to keep playing as if he was 24, not 41.

"Things will never be the same again. No matter what happens, no matter if he plays again or if you have a game to say goodbye to Ronaldo things will never be the same.

"What Ronaldo did for Portuguese football is unique and incredible and we must thank him for all the service he gave to Portugal. But at 41, he has no place in the best XI of Portugal."

Manager Jesus has reportedly said that he had not seen Ronaldo's statement as he was watching the Portugal Under-21s game.

Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.

It seems unlikely that Ronaldo will voluntarily retire from the national team before he hits the elusive 1,000-goal mark he is chasing for club and country - he currently has 979.

But have his actions made the situation untenable?

When it comes to fans, opinions appear to be split.

On several billboards in Lisbon posters have been put up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.

They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.

"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."

At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.

In stark contrast, Messi brought the curtain down on his illustrious Argentina career, where he has won one World Cup and two Copa Americas, in front of an 85,000-strong sellout crowd inside the Monumental in Buenos Aires.

The 39-year-old announced his retirement from international football in August after Argentina finished runners-up at the World Cup and following the death of his father Jorge.

Messi marked his final appearance for La Albiceleste with a goal before addressing the adoring fans in a speech lasting nearly 10 minutes.

Some of his team-mates were in tears as Messi admitted he did not want to leave the field.

"There are so many emotions going through me right now," he said. "I'm surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad.

"I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything."

Writing on social media on Wednesday, , externalMessi added: "Yesterday was my last match and I'm already missing the light blue and white jersey.

"I know I'm taking the right decision. It was an incredible journey, full of joy and some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it."

Messi also thanked his family, team-mates and clubs and paid tribute to another Argentina legend, the late Diego Maradona.

His Instagram post also drew a response from Ronaldo, who wrote: "Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever.

"I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug."

Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends

Messi departs as the record appearance-maker and goalscorer for Argentina but will continue his club career with Major League Soccer (MLS) team Inter Miami.

It seems the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner wants to enter the world of football club ownership and is making moves to do so.

He already owns two clubs - Spanish fifth-tier side UE Cornella and second-tier CD Eldense - as well as being a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa, which plans to open five branches in Catalonia.

Messi also has a lifetime deal with Adidas and a collection with drinkware brand Stanley as well as investing in the property and hotel industries.

Football expert Guillem Balague said: "Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.

"Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.

"Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game."

title: IMF chief urges governments to tighten belts as global debt levels soar
description: Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit...
fullText:
Kristalina Georgieva says big economies will have to make ‘very touch choices’ as soaring bond yields hit budgets

The head of the International Monetary Fund has called on governments across big economies to tighten their belts as soaring bond yields hit budgets.

Speaking in Singapore, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said global debt-to-GDP ratios were at their highest level since the second world war and on course to hit 100% in the coming years.

She said governments could not rely on rapid economic growth to lift the burden of debt – and instead would have to make “very tough political choices”.

Georgieva was speaking before the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, which are to be held in Bangkok next week. “My message to the world’s economic policymakers will be this: we cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them.

“And yet we don’t see decisive action in the high-debt advanced economies where the need of the hour is for credible medium-term fiscal consolidation plans, supported in some cases by upfront fiscal measures,” she said.

Bond yields – effectively the interest rate on the debt – have jumped in recent weeks, raising the cost of borrowing for many governments to multi-decade highs as markets adjust to the prospect of higher inflation as a result of the war in the Middle East.

“Elevated yields are inflating the interest bill at a time of tight budget constraints and competing spending priorities, including defence,” Georgieva said, calling for “an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses”.

The Bulgarian economist suggested central banks should be prepared to raise interest rates to see off resurgent inflation.

The ECB, US Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have already tightened policy in the face of rising inflation – moves Georgieva said were “highly appropriate” – but the Bank of England has so far left rates on hold at 3.75%.

“Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy,” Georgieva said, suggesting central banks might want to err on the side of caution.

She also stressed the importance of tackling some of the risks of AI, which has buoyed the US stock market but raised fears of mass layoffs.

She highlighted IMF research predicting that the adoption of AI could add half a percentage point to global economic growth if carried out effectively. However, she urged policymakers to “help manage AI’s substantial perils, including large-scale labour market fallout, serious cyber and stability risks and frontier models threatening to escape human control and run amok”.

The Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, who is also chair of the Financial Stability Forum that brings together the world’s central banks, recently warned of the “real and significant” risks posed by frontier AI models and called for the “right to intervene”.

In the UK the chancellor, John Healey, has said he will stick with his predecessor Rachel Reeves’s plans to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues – borrowing only to invest – and bring the debt-to-GDP ratio down over time.
